Due to variability in the clinical presentation, it is often challenging to distinguish MSA from PD, particularly in the early stages of presentation ( ). Urogenital symptoms are commonly reported in MSA, and lower urinary tract dysfunction can be the initial manifestation of MSA in 18% of patients ( ). The lumbosacral spinal cord is commonly affected in this condition, and autopsy studies have demonstrated degeneration in Onuf’s nucleus, a population of neurons in the anterior horn of the S2-4 segments ( ). Pathological changes have been shown to start early in the disease’s course ( ) and some patients may present initially with chronic urinary retention and sexual dysfunction suggesting a sacral cord onset of disease ( ). Neurogenic changes have been demonstrated in muscles innervated by Onuf’s nucleus, particularly the external anal sphincter ( ). The prevalence of neurogenic changes varies between 52% and 93% ( , , , , ) depending upon the patient cohort and neurophysiological parameter evaluated. Studies have shown that MUAP duration and the presence of spontaneous activity are the most reliable criteria in distinguishing MSA from other similar conditions, such as PD ( , , , , , ). There are challenges in interpreting the findings of anal sphincter EMG when trying to differentiate MSA from PD. The test will be normal if the Onuf’s nucleus has not been significantly affected yet and in one case series, abnormalities were seen in only 52–62% of cases in the first year after disease onset, which increased to 83% by the fifth year ( ). Furthermore, an abnormal result is not pathognomonic for MSA and neurogenic changes have also

The test will be normal if the Onuf’s nucleus has not been significantly affected yet and in one case series, abnormalities were seen in only 52–62% of cases in the first year after disease onset, which increased to 83% by the fifth year ( ). Furthermore, an abnormal result is not pathognomonic for MSA and neurogenic changes have also be reported in other disorders such as longstanding PD ( , ), Progressive Supranuclear Palsy ( , ), Dementia with Lewy Body ( ), Machado–Joseph disease, ( ) and Spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 ( ), suggesting that the Onuf’s nucleus can be affected in other disorders as well. However the degree of abnormalities are generally reported to be mild in these conditions, and occur later in the disease course. The utility of EMG in differentiating MSA from PD diminishes significantly over time, specially after five years of symptom onset ( , ). The criteria used to define abnormality also affects the accuracy of the test in differentiating MSA from PD ( , , ). A core issue is regarding the duration of MUAPs and whether to include or exclude satellite potentials—low-amplitude, delayed discharges that are time-locked to the MUAP and occur after it, with variable latency. Most published studies on EMG in MSA are retrospective studies that utilise data collected over several years in patients where the diagnosis is secure. Hence, the nature of MUAP potentials in the early stages of MSA remains unclear. Conventional wisdom suggests that a MUAP cut-off duration of 10 ms should be applied. Even though alternative or supplementary criteria have been suggested, such as adding polyphasic potentials, increased amplitude of more than 1 mV, or a percentage increase in either duration or polyphasics between 20 and 50% to the mean duration criteria, the widely used definition is a mean duration of MUAP greater than 10 ms to differentiate MSA from PD ( , , , ). However, when this criterion is applied to a case of suspected MSA, the outcome varies from completely normal to completely abnormal depending upon where the end cursor is placed, which introduces selection bias, as shown in . In this specific case, the test was repeated after two years and there were no differences seen in the EMG findings. At Queen Square we use the automated MUAP analysis mode and measure the MUAP duration without satellite potentials. Similar changes of denervation and reinnervation have also been recorded from the external urethral sphincter EMG ( , , ). However external anal sphincter EMG is more often performed as this test is better tolerated by the patients, is technically easier to perform and has published criteria that define abnormalities. In contrast to the sphincters, the bulbocavernosus muscle is not tonically active and therefore the muscle can be sampled to assess spontaneous activity. The BCR also assesses Onuf’s nucleus, and a prolonged latency or absent response has been demonstrated in patients reporting urogenital symptoms ( , , ). Patients with Fowler’s syndrome typically present in chronic urinary retention of more than a litre; however, they lack the sense of urinary urgency or bladder pain generally associated with such large volumes. When performing intermittent self-catheterisation, patients often report an abnormal sensation as if the catheter is being “gripped” when removed. A significant proportion of patients report polycystic ovaries ( ). Urethral sphincter EMG, urethral pressure profilometry and urethral sphincter volume have been demonstrated to be abnormal, suggesting that the condition is due to a primary disorder of urethral sphincter relaxation ( ). Spontaneously occurring fast-firing spontaneous discharges can be recorded from the external urethral sphincter EMG, and these include complex repetitive discharges (CRD), which are bizarre repetitively-firing highly symmetric bursts of variable frequency that have a characteristic sound similar to a helicopter over the loudspeaker of the EMG machine. Complex repetitive discharges may have a prominent decelerating component, called decelerating bursts, which have a myotonia-like quality ( , ). The frequency and rate of deceleration of these bursts have not been studied and they are recognisable by their characteristic sound over the loudspeaker, having a quality similar to the underwater recording of whales. The mechanisms responsible for urinary retention in this condition remains unclear. Complex repetitive discharges are non-specific findings of nerve injury and could suggest an increase in muscle fibre grouping from reinnervation and ephaptic transmission between muscle fibres ( ), possibly due to cryptic intramuscular nerve fibre injury or an unstable muscle membrane from a hormonally mediated channelopathy. Findings in urethral sphincter EMG and maximum urethral closure pressure have been shown to correlate ( ), and a pulsatile urethral pressure trace has been shown to be associated with decelerating bursts in the EMG ( ). Complex repetitive discharges have also been recorded from the external anal sphincter, suggesting that there could be wider pelvic floor dysfunction in some patients ( ). Complex repetitive discharges and decelerating bursts have also been recorded from the urethral sphincter of females not reporting urinary symptoms, more prevalent in the mid-luteal phase of the menstrual cycle ( , ). Therefore, the EMG findings should be interpreted in the clinical context of the patient. Diagnosing Fowler’s syndrome has therapeutic implications as patients have favourable outcomes following sacral neuromodulation ( ), the gold standard treatment for chronic idiopathic urinary retention in women, and botulinum toxin injected into the external urethral sphincter ( ). Pudendal afferents carry genital sensory information to the sacral cord and play a crucial role in modulating the sexual arousal response, and abnormalities in pudendal SEPs have been demonstrated in patients with erectile dysfunction when the somatic innervation has been injured ( , , , ). Abnormalities in the BCR have also been reported in men with erectile dysfunction ( , ). The neurophysiology of ejaculation involves both somatic and autonomic pathways ( ), and anejaculation has been reported following injury to the dorsal nerve of the penis ( ). Neurological lesions can affect sexual functions, and BCR and pudendal SEPs allow for the interrogation of the sacral reflex arc to localise the site of lesion and to plan management of sexual dysfunction ( ). The severity of sexual dysfunction following cauda equina injury has been shown to correlate with neurophysiological changes in the sacral reflex arc ( ). Erectile dysfunction in diabetic men has also been associated with abnormal findings in BCR and pudendal SEPs ( , ). Additionally, pudendal SEP abnormalities have been demonstrated in men and women with multiple sclerosis (MS) reporting sexual dysfunction ( , , ), suggesting a lesion affecting the DCML pathway. Unilateral dorsal nerve of the penis SEP studies have been shown to identify lesions more frequently than pudendal SEP ( ). Dynamic pudendal nerve compression from cycling can result in genital numbness and erectile dysfunction ( ). Sexual dysfunction has been reported following myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated demyelinating disease ( , , ) and with sacral Tarlov cysts ( ), where abnormalities in pelvic neurophysiology tests have been reported. Small nerve fibres play an important role in sexual function, including the perception of sexual sensations, erection, and ejaculation. Assessment of these fibres may be warranted when the aetiology of sexual dysfunction is unclear ( ). The association between the sympathetic skin response (SSR) and sexual dysfunction remains a matter of debate ( , ). However, in patients with diabetes, incorporating SSR into the neurophysiological evaluation can improve the detection rate of neurological abnormalities ( ). Furthermore, absence of the genital SSR has been linked to sexual dysfunction in women with multiple sclerosis ( ). Genital numbness can be reported in the context of sexual dysfunction, which could occur with central demyelinating lesions ( ), spinal cord injuries ( ), sacral root ( ) or peripheral nerve lesions. lists the different peripheral nerve lesions that can present with genital numbness. Lesions of the pudendal nerve and its branches ( ), illustrated in and described in , can cause genital numbness. However ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and genitofemoral nerves also contribute to the somatic innervation of the external genitalia and entrapment of these nerves can also present with genital numbness (illustrated in and described in ). Medications such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), isotretinoin and finasteride can also be associated with genital numbness and sexual dysfunction which may persist after the medications are discontinued ( , ). In these conditions, neurophysiology tests will be normal. Case vignette 6 illustrates a case of sexual dysfunction in a male patient. Case vignette 6. Sensations were normal over the glans. Other sexual domains were unaffected, and he did not report bladder or bowel symptoms. MRI lumbosacral spine showed only minor degenerative changes in the spine without any evidence for conus or cauda equina compression. He was referred for pelvic neurophysiology testing with the question whether there was a lesion affecting the pudendal nerve or sacral roots. Sensations were normal over the glans. Other sexual domains were unaffected, and he did not report bladder or bowel symptoms. MRI lumbosacral spine showed only minor degenerative changes in the spine without any evidence for conus or cauda equina compression. He was referred for pelvic neurophysiology testing with the question whether there was a lesion affecting the pudendal nerve or sacral roots. The neurological examination demonstrated a reduction in sensation to pinprick over the penis and anterior scrotum, and to light touch assessed using von Frey monofilament hairs on the ventral surface of the penis. The rest of the examination was unremarkable. Neurophysiology tests were abnormal ( ) and findings in the pudendal SEP and BCR tests are illustrated in , respectively. These findings confirmed a partial pudendal nerve lesion affecting the sensory fibres. MRI neurography study of the pelvis was normal and did not demonstrate entrapment of the pudendal nerve. Case vignette 7 illustrates a case of genital numbness in a female patient. Case vignette 7. Case of genital numbness in a female. A female in her mid-50s presented with genital numbness of 8 years duration. Symptoms began acutely following prolonged sitting on a static bicycle in the gym and the numbness was noticeable over the left side of the vulva involving the clitoris and labia. Numbness would worsen when sitting on hard seats, however at no point did she ever experience pain in the perineum. Sensations elsewhere were normal. MRI lumbosacral spine showed a central disc protrusion at L5/S1 level with a caudal migration compressing the left S2 root. An S2 root lesion could not explain her symptoms, and she was therefore referred for pelvic neurophysiology testing with the question whether there was any evidence for pudendal nerve injury or an S4 root injury. The neurological examination demonstrated a reduction in sensation to pinprick to 20% over the clitoris and the left labia minora. Light touch assessed using von Frey monofilament hairs was normal. The rest of the examination was unremarkable. The tests were abnormal ( ) and findings in the BCR test are illustrated in . These findings confirmed a partial injury of the left side pudendal nerve, with likely localisation distal to the inferior rectal branch. MRI neurography study of the pelvis was normal and did not demonstrate entrapment of the pudendal nerve. 3.6 Evaluation of chronic pelvic pain The term pudendal neuralgia is often used synonymously with chronic pelvic pain. However, chronic pelvic pain can result from involvement of a number of different nerves such as the ilioinguinal ( ), genitofemoral ( ), posterior femoral cutaneous ( ) or iliohypogastric ( ) nerves. Pain can also originate from the pelvic viscera when stretched or overdistended from signalling through the visceral afferent pathways ( ). In addition, visceral or dermatomal afferent signals can influence somatic efferent pathways at the spinal cord through cross-organ sensitisation ( ). The ilioinguinal nerve exits the inguinal canal and injury can result in pain over the anterior labia /scrotum. The perineal branch of the pudendal nerve is responsible for sensations over the medial labia, whereas the dorsal clitoris/ penile nerve is responsible for sensations over the clitoris /penis, and the perineal branch of the posterior cutaneous nerve is responsible for sensations over the one fifth of the labia majora ( ). Injuries to these nerves may present as chronic pelvic pain in the respective nerve territories. lists the different peripheral nerve lesions that can present with genital pain. Peripheral nerve entrapment can present with genital pain (illustrated in , and described in ). Injury to the inferior rectal nerve can present with perianal pain ( , ). Ilioinguinal nerve damage can also present with genital pain, mainly at the root of the penis or clitoris, scrotum /labia and upper medial thigh. The nerve mainly originates from the spinal nerve L1 and emerges at the Anterior Superior Iliac Spine (ASIS). It pierces the transversus abdominis muscle and travels through the inguinal canal, and gives off its terminal sensory branches to the genital region. Normal motor conduction is demonstrated in . The nerve can be damaged following surgical incisions or suture entrapment, resulting in pain in the genital region which can be mistaken as clitoral pain. Dysfunction of any of these nerves can result in non-specific debilitating pain that can often be mistaken as pudendal neuralgia and testing of the pudendal nerve alone may miss the nerve injury. A thorough clinical examination is essential to map out the distribution of pain in the distribution of a dermatome or nerve territory. Case vignette 8 illustrates a case of pudendal neuralgia. Dysfunction of any of these nerves can result in non-specific debilitating pain that can often be mistaken as pudendal neuralgia and testing of the pudendal nerve alone may miss the nerve injury. A thorough clinical examination is essential to map out the distribution of pain in the distribution of a dermatome or nerve territory. Case vignette 8 illustrates a case of pudendal neuralgia. Case vignette 8. Case of pudendal neuralgia. A female in her 70 s presented with pain in the perineum that started around 4 years prior. She described the pain as having a “twisting” quality, similar to a spasm, occurring in relation to the opening of the vagina and back passage which extended into the vagina and rectum. The pain would become worse within minutes of sitting down, though she did not experience pain when seated on the toilet. She was being treated for atrophic vulvovaginitis. MRI of the thoracolumbar spine revealed a mid-thoracic cord syrinx and no enhancement was noted with gadolinium administration. She was referred for pelvic neurophysiology testing with the question whether the syrinx was compressing the sacral fibres within the dorsal column. Her symptoms were typical for pudendal neuralgia, and a second question was whether there was any evidence for pudendal nerve injury. The pelvic neurological examination demonstrated patchy, inconsistent sensory impairment over the S2, S3 and S4 dermatomes bilaterally. The neurophysiology tests were abnormal ( ) and findings of the left pudendal SEP test are illustrated in . These findings confirmed an injury of the left side pudendal nerve affecting the sensory and motor fibres. MRI neurography study of the pelvis was normal and did not demonstrate entrapment of the pudendal nerve. There was no neurophysiological evidence of compression of the dorsal column by the syrinx. 3.7 Evaluation of voiding dysfunction Urodynamics testing is designed to investigate lower urinary tract symptoms to evaluate how well the bladder and urethral sphincter function during bladder filling and emptying. Kinesiologic EMG recording performed concomitantly with urodynamic testing has been used to assess sphincter activity, particularly to recognise detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia (DSD). This is a characteristic abnormality seen in patients reporting lower urinary tract dysfunction following SCI where there is concomitant contraction of the detrusor and external urethral sphincter during attempted voiding. Detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia is an important cause of voiding dysfunction and urinary retention ( ) and is important to recognise, being a risk factor for developing renal impairment ( ). In health, EMG activity in the external urethral sphincter ceases during voiding, whereas in patients with DSD, EMG activity persists or increases due to increased recruitment of motor units during attempted voiding ( ). Early studies introduced external urethral sphincter concentric needle recording into urodynamics practice and defined DSD as increased EMG activity during a detrusor contraction ( ). Inappropriate contraction or failure of relaxation of either the internal (smooth muscle) and/or external (striated muscle) urethral sphincter concomitant with detrusor contraction was demonstrated with simultaneous recording of external urethral sphincter activity by EMG ( ). EMG activity was also recorded from the external anal sphincter using monopolar needles, and DSD was defined as increased anal sphincter activity when instructed to void or perform a Valsalva manoeuvre ( ). However a similar pattern of sphincter activity mimicking DSD can be recorded with voluntary contraction of the external sphincter by uncooperative patients, or in case of learned abnormal behaviours in patients presenting with dysfunctional voiding such as in Hinman’s syndrome with a non-neurogenic neurogenic bladder ( ). Using a concentric needle can be uncomfortable for patients, and therefore surface electrodes are generally preferred. However, the amplitude of EMG activity recorded from surface electrodes is smaller because of interposed adipose tissue, and the signal quality can be contaminated by artifacts from 50 Hz electromagnetic interference and electrode displacement from insufficient skin adhesion due to moisture or, in females, the urinary stream tracking down the perineum ( ). The International Continence Society (ICS) guidelines on urodynamic equipment standardisation recommend that EMG recordings during urodynamics should adhere to specific criteria, including a high input impedance exceeding 100 megaohms, a common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) greater than 80 and the incorporation of a filtering program. These specifications aim to optimise the consistency of EMG recordings during the testing ( ). However despite this, published statements regarding EMG technique and reporting vary considerably. This is partly due to the evolving definition of DSD, and because the established neurophysiology techniques which are nowadays used for diagnosing DSD have not been adapted to modern-day consensus definitions. Nowadays, the diagnosis of DSD is increasingly being established by fluoroscopy performed during urodynamic testing (videourodynamics testing), however kinesiologic EMG

a high input impedance exceeding 100 megaohms, a common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) greater than 80 and the incorporation of a filtering program. These specifications aim to optimise the consistency of EMG recordings during the testing ( ). However despite this, published statements regarding EMG technique and reporting vary considerably. This is partly due to the evolving definition of DSD, and because the established neurophysiology techniques which are nowadays used for diagnosing DSD have not been adapted to modern-day consensus definitions. Nowadays, the diagnosis of DSD is increasingly being established by fluoroscopy performed during urodynamic testing (videourodynamics testing), however kinesiologic EMG recording still has a role in centres where facilities for performing such urodynamics studies are lacking. 4 Conclusion Pelvic neurophysiology testing offers a unique means of assessing the segmental somatic innervation of the sacral spinal cord (S2–S4), and uncover patterns of nerve injury not apparent through imaging, laboratory studies and other functional tests alone. Given the complexity and invasive nature of some of the tests, they should be performed with a clear clinical question that guides test selection and interpretation. These tests provide objective evidence of nerve dysfunction and are particularly valuable in specific scenarios, such as the evaluation of suspected cauda equina syndrome, MSA, chronic urinary retention, pelvic pain, sexual dysfunction and situations where MRI findings are inconclusive. When used as an adjunct to clinical examination, neurophysiological testing enhances diagnostic accuracy in the assessment of patients with neuro-urological disorders. documents.title: AUA Microhematuria Diagnosis Evaluation Follow-up Guideline

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Differentiating between glomerular hematuria (GH) and nonglomerular hematuria (NGH) is essential because persistent glomerular hematuria correlates with a heightened risk of terminal kidney failure, particularly in younger patients [ , ]. According to the EFLM urinalysis guidelines, the differentiation between glomerular and nonglomerular hematuria requires the detection of dysmorphic red blood cells (RBCs) using microscopic examination [ ]. Indeed, for nearly 70 years, the detection of glomerular hematuria has relied predominantly on microscopic examination of dysmorphic red blood cells (RBCs) [ , ]. However, this method poses several challenges, including difficulties in standardization, substantial labor demands, and reliance on the expertise of trained examiners [ , ]. In our study, we investigated the urine red blood cell distribution (URD), defined as the percentage of small RBC fractions [ ], which is automatically measured using the Sysmex UF‐5000 analyzer. The URD parameter demonstrated diagnostic performance (area under the curve, AUC = 0.68–0.83) comparable to that of dysmorphic RBC analysis (AUC = 0.73–0.79) for distinguishing between glomerular and nonglomerular hematuria. Moreover, URD offers notable advantages, including objectivity, reproducibility, time efficiency, and automation, thus serving as a more practical alternative [ , , , ]. Given that URD results are quantitative and objective, we aimed to enhance their diagnostic performance by incorporating additional renal parameters associated with glomerular function. Urine protein (dipstick) and serum creatinine were selected, as both are routinely used as screening tests for assessing glomerular integrity. URD values were reclassified into five levels, and the UPC index (URD plus protein‐strip and creatinine) was developed by combining these categorized URD values with corresponding urine protein and serum creatinine levels. The UPC index was expected to more accurately reflect glomerular hematuria compared to URD alone, as both urine protein and serum creatinine are strongly associated with glomerular function. To assess the diagnostic performance of UPC, we conducted a retrospective study across three university hospitals. Although the URD parameter demonstrates diagnostic performance comparable to dysmorphic RBC analysis, URD alone has inherent limitations in fully reflecting the severity of hematuria, particularly in patients with glomerular diseases [ , , , ]. If UPC indexes demonstrate superior diagnostic performance compared to dysmorphic RBC analysis, the clinical utility of UPC—which offers objective, standardized, and reproducible results—is anticipated to increase significantly. 2 Materials and Methods 2.1 Study Subjects This study included 813 patients who visited three tertiary medical centers in Korea (D: 332 patients, P: 124 patients, S: 357 patients) between December 2022 and December 2023. All subjects underwent renal function evaluations as part of routine clinical practice. The study design is illustrated in Figure . Fasting blood and random urine samples were collected from each subject. On the basis of renal biopsy results or clinical diagnoses, the patients were classified into four groups: glomerular diseases (GD), renal diseases (RD), extrarenal diseases (ERD), and isolated hematuria (IH). Patients were classified according to the primary clinical or pathological diagnosis at the time of index urinalysis (Table ). The renal diseases group included acute kidney injury (AKI), chronic kidney disease (CKD), nephrotic syndrome (NS), and tubulointerstitial disease (TID) based on Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Guidelines [ , ]. While most renal disease cases were diagnosed clinically, among 285 patients classified as having GD, 236 (82.8%) underwent kidney biopsies. For the evaluation of screening performance, we compared patients with GD and ERD as surrogate groups for GH and NGH, respectively. This approach was adopted to ensure a reliable and conservative reference standard, as most GD cases were biopsy‐confirmed. The clinically diagnosed RD group was excluded from the comparison group because GH and NGH mechanisms may coexist and biopsy confirmation is often unavailable. In addition, the distributions of UPC, URD, ACR, and PCR values were analyzed within the renal diseases group. 2.2 Urine Parameter Measurements URD and urine particle analysis were performed using the fully automated UF‐5000 urine particle analyzer (Sysmex Corporation, Kobe, Japan) at the D, P, and S medical centers. Urinary protein, albumin, and creatinine concentrations were measured using the COBAS C702 analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland) at the S and D medical centers, and the AU5800 analyzer (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA) at the P medical center. The assay methods and reagents used for urine chemical analyses are summarized in Table . The urinary albumin‐to‐creatinine ratio (ACR) and protein‐to‐creatinine ratio (PCR) were calculated by dividing the urinary albumin or protein concentrations by the corresponding urine creatinine concentration. Urine strip analysis was conducted using the UC 3500 analyzer (Sysmex Corporation, Kobe, Japan) at the P and S medical centers and the Uriscan Super+ analyzer (YD Diagnostics, Yongin, Korea) at the D medical center. All urine particles and chemical analyses were completed within 30 min of specimen receipt to ensure accuracy and reliability. 2.3 Serum Parameter Measurements Levels of total serum protein, albumin, creatinine, and blood

urine chemical analyses are summarized in Table . The urinary albumin‐to‐creatinine ratio (ACR) and protein‐to‐creatinine ratio (PCR) were calculated by dividing the urinary albumin or protein concentrations by the corresponding urine creatinine concentration. Urine strip analysis was conducted using the UC 3500 analyzer (Sysmex Corporation, Kobe, Japan) at the P and S medical centers and the Uriscan Super+ analyzer (YD Diagnostics, Yongin, Korea) at the D medical center. All urine particles and chemical analyses were completed within 30 min of specimen receipt to ensure accuracy and reliability. 2.3 Serum Parameter Measurements Levels of total serum protein, albumin, creatinine, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) were measured using chemical analyzers at the D, P, and S medical centers. The COBAS C702 analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland) was utilized at the D and S medical centers, while the AU5800 analyzer (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA) was employed at the P medical center. Detailed assay principles and reagent information are provided in Table . The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated using the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD‐EPI 2021) formula. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were retrospectively, sequentially extracted from the patients' electronic medical records. The exclusion criteria were samples with ≤ 20 RBC/μL, insufficient clinical information, and patients with heart valve prostheses or thrombotic microangiopathy. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at each participating center (CR‐23‐019‐L), and the requirement for obtaining informed consent was waived. 2.4 <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">URD</styled-content>, Protein‐Strip, and Creatinine (<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">UPC</styled-content>) Parameters The UPC index was developed by integrating URD, urine protein (dipstick), and serum creatinine values. URD results were categorized into five ordinal groups (0–4) based on the previous study [ ]: ≤ 31.9% (grade 0), 32.0%–44.9% (grade 1), 45.0%–58.9% (grade 2), 60.0%–78.9% (grade 3), and ≥ 80.0% (grade 4). Urine protein levels were similarly scored on a 0–4 scale corresponding to dipstick readings (negative, trace (0.5), 1+, 2+, 3+). Serum creatinine was incorporated directly into the index with one modification: for values ≤ 5.0 mg/dL, the actual value was used; for values > 5.0 mg/dL, a fixed value of 5.0 was applied to prevent disproportionate influence on the composite score. The UPC index was calculated using the following formula: UPC = URD grade + Urine protein grade + Serum creatinine , where creatinine = creatinine (≤ 5.0) or 5.0 (if creatinine > 5.0). To validate this scoring approach, both univariate and multivariate binary logistic regression analyses were performed. Each of the three parameters—URD, urine protein, and creatinine—demonstrated significant and independent predictive value for glomerular hematuria (data not shown). Although the odds ratios varied, an equal‐weight additive model was adopted to ensure clinical interpretability and ease of implementation. 2.5 Validation of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">UPC</styled-content> Index Internal validation of the UPC index was conducted using 5‐fold cross‐validation, stratified by GD and ERD groups. The analysis was performed using Python ( www.python.org ). The mean area under the curve (AUC) was 0.851 with a standard deviation of 0.018, indicating consistent and robust discriminative performance of the UPC index. 2.6 Comparison of Urine and Serum Parameters for Differential Diagnosis between Glomerular Hematuria (<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">GH</styled-content>) and Nonglomerular Hematuria (<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">NGH</styled-content>) The diagnostic efficacy of UPC, URD, and other urine and serum parameters was evaluated by comparing their area under the curve (AUC) values for distinguishing GD from ERD. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to determine these values. 2.7 Statistical Analysis Descriptive data were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges, while categorical variables were expressed as counts and percentages. The diagnostic performance of laboratory parameters in predicting GH was assessed through ROC curve analysis, with AUC values and 95% confidence intervals calculated to differentiate GH from NGH. Categorical variables were compared using the chi‐square test, and continuous variables were analyzed using the Kruskal–Wallis test. The significance level of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed using MedCalc software (version 12.7.0.0; MedCalc Software Ltd, Ostend, Belgium). 3 Results 3.1 Patient and Laboratory Characteristics Among the 813 patients, 437 (53.8%) were female, and 376 (46.2%) were male, with a median age of 64.0 years (interquartile range: 51.0–77.0). Detailed patient characteristics and laboratory results are presented in Table . Significant differences in age, UPC, URD, ACR, PCR, BUN, Cr, and eGFR were observed among the seven patient groups. The median UPC indexes were higher in patients with NS, CKD, AKI, and GD (5.8, 5.7, 5.6, and 5.6, respectively) than in patients with TID, ERD, and IH (3.4, 2.6, and 4.3 respectively). Similarly, the median values of URD were higher in patients with NS (73.8%), GD (75.7%), and IH (63.7%) than in patients with TID (25.9%) and ERD (22.1%). Median ACR and PCR values were most pronounced in patients with NS, followed by GD and CKD. Conversely, the highest median BUN and

in age, UPC, URD, ACR, PCR, BUN, Cr, and eGFR were observed among the seven patient groups. The median UPC indexes were higher in patients with NS, CKD, AKI, and GD (5.8, 5.7, 5.6, and 5.6, respectively) than in patients with TID, ERD, and IH (3.4, 2.6, and 4.3 respectively). Similarly, the median values of URD were higher in patients with NS (73.8%), GD (75.7%), and IH (63.7%) than in patients with TID (25.9%) and ERD (22.1%). Median ACR and PCR values were most pronounced in patients with NS, followed by GD and CKD. Conversely, the highest median BUN and Cr levels were observed in patients with AKI and CKD. 3.2 Comparison of Renal Function Parameters for Differential Diagnosis between Glomerular and Extrarenal Diseases ROC curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of renal function parameters in distinguishing GD from ERD (Figure ). Among the parameters, the AUC values were highest for UPC (0.857), followed by URD (0.779), ACR (0.746), PCR (0.648), Cr (0.555), and BUN (0.528). Notably, the AUC value of UPC was significantly higher compared to all other parameters (Table ). The cut‐off values, sensitivities, and specificities for the renal function parameters are summarized in Table . UPC demonstrated the highest sensitivity (86.7%) and specificity (73.1%) among the evaluated parameters, underscoring its superior diagnostic utility. 3.3 Comparison of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">UPC</styled-content>, <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">URD</styled-content>, <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ACR</styled-content>, and <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PCR</styled-content> Results Among Patients with <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">RD</styled-content> (<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CKD</styled-content>, <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">AKI</styled-content>, <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">NS,</styled-content> and <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">TID</styled-content>) The results of UPC, URD, ACR, and PCR were analyzed among patients with four renal diseases (Figure ). The UPC indexes showed a significant difference between the CKD, AKI, and NS groups (ranging from 5.6 to 5.8) and the TID group (3.4; p < 0.05). URD values also revealed significant differences between the AKI and NS groups compared to TID; however, no significant difference was observed between CKD (46.6%) and TID (25.9%). ACR demonstrated significant differences between CKD and NS groups versus TID, but no significant difference was found between AKI (196.5 mg/g) and TID (129.7 mg/g). PCR did not show significant differences among the four renal disease groups. 3.4 Correlation of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">UPC</styled-content> Indexes with Renal Parameters Correlation analysis (Table ) revealed that UPC was significantly correlated with URD (0.676), ACR (0.461), PCR (0.408), creatinine (0.325), and BUN (0.237). In comparison, URD exhibited a weak correlation with creatinine (−0.187) and BUN (−0.119) and showed no correlation with ACR and PCR. Both ACR and PCR demonstrated significant correlations with other renal parameters ( p < 0.001), with the exception of URD. 4 Discussion Microhematuria is defined as the presence of more than three RBC per high‐power field on microscopic evaluation of a single urine specimen. Patients presenting with microhematuria should undergo repeated urinalysis to assess for potential genitourinary malignancies or glomerular injury [ , ]. A key step in the evaluation of microhematuria involves microscopic examination of urinary sediment to differentiate between GH and NGH [ ]. RBCs in hematuria are classified as isomorphic or dysmorphic. Isomorphic RBCs typically indicate bleeding from the urinary tract, while dysmorphic RBCs suggest glomerular bleeding [ , ]. In older individuals, common causes of hematuria include urinary tract infections, various urological malignancies, urolithiasis, postinfectious and other types of glomerulonephritis, trauma, prostatic enlargement, and urinary instrumentation [ ]. However, in approximately 50% of cases, no definitive etiology is identified [ ]. Studies investigating hematuria in adult populations have reported an overall incidence of urinary tract cancer of approximately 10.0% [ , ]. When hematuria is accompanied by proteinuria, urinary casts, or dysmorphic RBCs, it is strongly indicative of underlying glomerular disease [ ]. Although age and sex were not matched among the seven groups presented in Table , these discrepancies are unlikely to have significantly influenced the results, given the minimal impact of age and sex on renal function parameters in the context of this study [ ]. The distinction between GH and NGH is ideally based on pathophysiological mechanisms, with renal biopsy serving as the reference standard. However, in routine clinical practice, biopsy is not performed in the majority of patients with hematuria, particularly those with suspected NGH. In this context, we intentionally applied a conservative analytical framework by using biopsy‐confirmed GD as a surrogate for GH and ERD as representative of NGH. This strategy was designed to minimize misclassification and overestimation of diagnostic performance. Compared to ERD patients, UPC and URD values were significantly elevated in GD suggesting UPC and URD are reliable markers for differentiating GH and NGH. While compared to IH patients, the patients of CKD, GD, and NS showed higher median UPC indexes than those with IH. But the patients with CKD and AKI revealed lower median URD values than those of IH. These

In this context, we intentionally applied a conservative analytical framework by using biopsy‐confirmed GD as a surrogate for GH and ERD as representative of NGH. This strategy was designed to minimize misclassification and overestimation of diagnostic performance. Compared to ERD patients, UPC and URD values were significantly elevated in GD suggesting UPC and URD are reliable markers for differentiating GH and NGH. While compared to IH patients, the patients of CKD, GD, and NS showed higher median UPC indexes than those with IH. But the patients with CKD and AKI revealed lower median URD values than those of IH. These findings suggest that UPC serves as a more reliable indicator than URD for distinguishing glomerular from nonglomerular hematuria. This is primarily because (1) the most common causes of hematuria are of nonglomerular origin [ ], and (2) CKD and AKI frequently involve glomerular injuries [ , , ]. In the groups of renal diseases (Figure ), the UPC indexes showed significant differences between the CKD, AKI, and NS groups compared to the TID group, whereas the URD values did not significantly differ between CKD and TID. Therefore, the UPC parameter proved more effective in differentiating TID from other renal disease subtypes. Since CKD, AKI, and NS are considered GD, these findings suggest that URD has limitations in distinguishing GH from NGH. As demonstrated in Figure and Table , UPC exhibited the highest AUC values, along with superior sensitivity and specificity, for distinguishing GD from ERD. Its high sensitivity (86.7%) makes UPC particularly valuable as a screening tool for GH. While URD achieved better AUC values than ACR, these differences were not statistically significant. In the correlation analysis, UPC displayed statistically significant correlations with other renal parameters, including ACR, PCR, creatinine, and BUN, whereas URD showed weaker correlations with creatinine and BUN. These findings indicate that UPC provides a more accurate reflection of renal function compared to URD. This study is not without limitations. As a retrospective study, the diagnosis of renal diseases was reliant on medical records, which may introduce biases. Additionally, the original data was not specifically collected for research purposes, raising the potential for selection and recall biases [ ]. In summary, UPC demonstrated: (1) the highest AUC values for differentiating glomerular from extrarenal hematuria, (2) a significant difference between the CKD, AKI, NS groups and the TID group, and (3) significant correlations with ACR, PCR, creatinine, and BUN. These findings collectively suggest that UPC is a more reliable indicator than URD for differentiating glomerular from nonglomerular hematuria. Funding The authors have nothing to report. chunks.content: Introduction Upper urinary calculi are among the common clinical urological diseases, with a prevalence that is increasing worldwide, and 95% of cases occur in the kidneys and ureters [ ]. Common clinical symptoms include pain and haematuria. Some patients may also experience severe pain, which makes it impossible to continue working and affects daily life, causing serious damage to physical and mental health [ , ]. Most upper urinary calculi are treated with surgery. Surgical removal of the stones relieves pain and improves symptoms such as haematuria, nausea, and vomiting [ , ]. Previous studies have shown that among the various complications related to upper urinary calculi, urosepsis is characterised by its sudden onset, rapid progression, and potentially dangerous conditions [ ]. If it is not treated promptly and effectively, it can further progress to septic shock. In cases of multiple organ dysfunction, the condition can rapidly deteriorate and become uncontrollable, with a fatality rate as high as 20% to 40% [ ]. The European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) and the American Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM) updated the definition of sepsis in 2016, which was defined as a dysfunctional host response to infection leading to life-threatening organ dysfunction [ ]. The common causes of urosepsis mainly include systemic and local factors, with systemic risk factors primarily comprising advanced age, female sex, diabetes, and immunosuppression [ , ]. Local risk factors primarily involve urinary tract obstruction, with urinary calculi being the most common [ ]. Risk prediction models for urosepsis combine multiple predictive factors to estimate the probability of urosepsis occurrence, including factors derived from patient demographics, clinical history, physical examination, disease characteristics, test results, and previous treatments [ ]. Upper urinary calculi can rapidly progress to acute-onset urosepsis and dangerous conditions, necessitating timely and effective treatment [ ]. Although the number of studies on predictive models for postoperative urosepsis complications in patients with upper urinary calculi is increasing, no models have yet been validated for clinical practice, and the methodological quality of these studies requires further evaluation. Consequently, we conducted a systematic review with meta-analysis to identify predictive factors for urosepsis and systematically review the literature on the predictive modeling of postoperative complications associated with urinary sepsis in patients with upper urinary calculi. Methods The review protocol was registered on PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42024596003). Search strategy A comprehensive search was undertaken in the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang, PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, EMBASE, and EBSCO databases, which were searched from the inception of the databases until October 17, 2024., and using the following keywords: (“Urinary Calculi”[MeSH] or “Kidney Calculus”[MeSH] or “Ureteral Calculus”[MeSH]) and “urosepsis” and (“Risk prediction model” or “Predictor” or “Model” and “Risk Score”. Detailed search strategies can be found in Appendix A. The present meta-analysis was conducted according to the guidelines in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses statement (PRISMA) [ ]. The main items reviewed by our system are described as follows: P (population): Patients with upper urinary calculi complicated with postoperative urosepsis. I (intervention model): A published model was developed to predict the risk of urosepsis in patients after upper urinary tract stone surgery (predictors ≥ 2). C (comparator): No competing model. O (outcome): The results of the review focused on the group with postoperative urosepsis rather than its subgroups. T (timing): Outcomes were predicted after evaluation of basic information and laboratory indicators at admission. S (setting): The intended use of the risk prediction model is to individually predict the occurrence of uraemia in patients after upper urinary tract calculus surgery and to provide a framework for developing and refining an early warning assessment tool for postoperative urosepsis. Inclusion and exclusion criteria The inclusion criteria for the studies were as follows: (1) involved patients after surgery for urinary calculi, which included kidney and ureteral stones; (2) the study objective was to develop predictive models, with the requirement that each model must include at least two predictive factors; (3) the models were evaluated using metrics such as Area Under the Curve (AUC) values. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) studies in which a predictive model was not established; (2) studies in which only the occurrence of urosepsis after surgery was used as a subgroup result; and (3) studies not written in English or Chinese. Selection and screening Two researchers (JYW, RW) trained in evidence-based methodology independently screened the literature and extracted the data. These researchers first read the titles and abstracts of the articles as part of preliminary screening and then read the full texts to determine the final included literature. After that, the two researchers exchanged their findings to assess consistency. When there were differences of opinion, they discussed the matter with a third author (XFC) before reaching a decision. Data extraction Article information

These researchers first read the titles and abstracts of the articles as part of preliminary screening and then read the full texts to determine the final included literature. After that, the two researchers exchanged their findings to assess consistency. When there were differences of opinion, they discussed the matter with a third author (XFC) before reaching a decision. Data extraction Article information was extracted by two researchers (FW, XTZ) trained in systematic evidence-based nursing. The extracted information from the selected studies was divided into two categories: (1) basic information of the literature, including the author, country, publication year, study design type, study objects, data sources, sample size, main outcomes, and other details; and (2) model information, including details related to the prediction model, such as variable selection methods, model development methods, model verification types, model performance measures, handling of missing data, methods for processing continuous variables, final predictors used in the model, and the format in which the model is presented. After the information is extracted, both researchers conduct a final check to ensure the accuracy of the data. Quality assessment and risk of bias To assess the quality and potential risk of bias in the included studies, we utilised the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST) [ ] to evaluate four areas: the study objects, the predictors, the results, and the statistical analysis. PROBAST includes 20 signalling questions assessed by two independent reviewers (CLZ, JYW). Each signalling question is answered with one of the following options: yes, probably yes, no, probably no, or no information. The evaluation results for each area are categorised as low, high, or unclear. Discrepancies in the ratings were resolved through discussion with a third reviewer. Data statistical analysis A meta-analysis of predictors was conducted via Stata (version 17.0; Stata Corporation, College Station, Texas, USA). Refer to previous studies [ , ] a meta-analysis of AUC values and their 95% CIs was conducted, which allowed for quantifying model performance via AUC and revealing uncertainty ranges with the 95% CIs, enabling a comprehensive assessment of model stability. Since the AUC does not rely on the selection of a specific classification threshold, it can more stably reflect the model’s overall discriminatory power. Additionally, when combined with the 95% CI, it enables quantification of the uncertainty in the estimate. The Cochrane Q test and I² index were used to assess heterogeneity among the included studies. If P > 0.1 and I² < 50%, heterogeneity was considered acceptable, and a fixed-effects model was applied. Conversely, if I 2 ≥ 50% or P ≤ 0.1, heterogeneity among the studies was considered significant, prompting the performance of sensitivity analyses. After studies were excluded one by one, if heterogeneity persisted, a random effects model was used for merging. If the combined effect size did not change significantly, the results of the meta-analysis were considered stable. Egger’s test was used to identify publication bias. A P value greater than 0.05 indicates a low likelihood of publication bias [ ]. Results Search results A total of 573 records were obtained from seven Chinese and English databases. After assessment using EndNote 20, 67 duplicates were removed, and 62 records were excluded by screening the titles and abstracts. Among the remaining 444 records, screening against the inclusion and exclusion criteria resulted in the inclusion of 25 studies [ , , – ]. Figure shows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) 2020, depicting the comprehensive search process and results. Characteristics of the included studies Among the 25 studies included, 12 were in Chinese and 13 were in English. The included studies were published between 2017 and 2024. However, 23 of these studies had data sources from China. The 20 studies were retrospective case‒control studies (including 1 multicentre study), 3 cohort studies (including 2 multicentre studies), 1 nested case‒control study, and 1 prospective cohort study. Regarding the study type, 8 studies focused on development and validation models. In terms of population, the study focused on patients with upper urinary calculi, including kidney calculi and ureteral calculi, and those who underwent percutaneous nephrolithotomy met the inclusion criteria. The sample size for the study ranged from 114 to 2,066 participants; the prevalence of urinary sepsis ranged from 1.65% to 50%. Modelling methods include binary logistic regression models, multiple logistic regression, LASSO regression, random forest, machine learning, bayesian classifiers, gaussian weighted classifiers, and support vector machines. The models reported in the included studies were either internally or externally validated. External validation was performed in 10 studies, and internal validation was performed in 11 studies. An additional three studies [ , , ] included both internal and external validation. In addition, the study was validated via a Monte Carlo cross-validation scheme [ ]. For model development, the predictive performance of the model was evaluated in terms of both discrimination and calibration. Distinctiveness was mainly expressed by the area under the curve (AUC) or the consistency index (C-index) of the subjects’ work characteristics, and calibration was comprehensively evaluated using the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test (H-L test) and by plotting the calibration graphs. Twenty-five studies evaluated the performance of the models, and 12 studies only reported the discriminant metrics and not the calibration metrics. All the models built in the included studies had a discriminant index > 0.7, indicating that the models had good predictive performance. Predictive factors of the included models The number of predictors ultimately included in each predictive model ranged from 2 to 10, covering 39 different factors contributing to postoperative urinary sepsis. The predictors included in the model were divided into four main categories: (1) Basic patient conditions: sex, age, diabetes mellitus status, history of ipsilateral urologic surgery, functional isolated kidney, ureteral stenosis, preoperative renal fistula, long stent time, STONE score, renal pyogenesis, history of lumbago and abdominal pain, and renal anatomic malformation; (2) Surgery-related conditions: days of preoperative antibiotic use, intraoperative hypotension, operation time and increased irrigation rate; (3) Information on ancillary medical examinations: temperature, urine culture, urine white blood cell count, urine nitrite levels, platelet count, fibrinogen levels, neutrophil count, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, hypoproteinaemia, C-reactive protein levels, white blood cell count, procalcitonin levels, urine glucose levels, accumulated time of renal pelvic pressure, degree of hydronephrosis, and mean CT value of hydronephrosis; (4) Upper urinary calculi factors: larger stone burden, infectious calculi, stone diameter, ureteral calculus location, number of stones, staghorn stones, and degree of stone clearance. Figure shows the frequency of predictors. Model presentation of the included models All the studies reported the presentation of the model, with 16 studies presenting a nomogram model, 4 studies presenting modelled equations, and 1 study presenting both column‒line plots and modelled equations. In addition, there were 2 random forest models and 2 machine learning models. Risk of bias of included studies The risk of bias and applicability of the 25 included studies were evaluated using the PROBAST literature quality assessment tool (Appendix A). In the participant domain, the bias related to study participants primarily stems from the type of study conducted. Four models [ , , , ] were considered to have a low risk of bias. The remainder were evaluated as having a high risk of bias mainly because the studies were retrospective case‒control studies. In the predictor domain, all models were graded as having a high risk of bias because none of the included predictors mentioned blinding, and we responded with a rating of ‘probably yes’. In the outcome domain, three models [ , , ] were considered to be at high risk of bias because standard or consensus definitions of outcomes were not used. With respect to the analysis domain, all of the models considered to have a high risk of bias reported processing details for missing values, which led to an overall evaluation judgement of a high risk of bias. In terms of the assessment of applicability, two models [ , ] were classified as high risk bias, and the remainder were classified as low risk bias. The review by [ ] included patients who developed uraemia and required admission to the intensive care unit, who we considered to be at high risk bias. The study population in [ ] specifically included diabetic patients, which diverged from the population of the present study and was judged by a third party to be a high-risk offset. The remaining models were evaluated as having a low risk in all areas and overall. Meta-analysis results Among the 25 studies included, 12 models did not report the AUC or the 95% CI. 1 models

The remaining models were evaluated as having a low risk in all areas and overall. Meta-analysis results Among the 25 studies included, 12 models did not report the AUC or the 95% CI. 1 models [ ] was excluded due to the use of random forest and did not report the calculus location results and were excluded. A meta-analysis was performed on the data from 12 models [ , , , , , , , , – ] in the remaining studies. The pooled AUC, which was calculated using a random effects model, was 0.90 (95% CI: 0.87, 0.93), indicating good predictive performance (Fig. ). The I 2 value was 73.4% ( P < 0.001), indicating a high degree of heterogeneity among the studies. After subgroup analyses to explore the sources of heterogeneity, the pooled AUC showed relatively good stability regarding study design (AUC = 0.92, I² > 50%) and participants (AUC = 0.92, I² > 50%), heterogeneity remained significant. For the subgroup analysis, forest plots were provided to show the association between patient risk factors and postoperative urinary tract infection incidence, which were expressed as odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals (Figs. and ). A total of 39 predictors leading to postoperative urinary sepsis were covered in the 25 included studies. Details are provided in Table . Further meta-analysis of the 20 predictors revealed that urine culture [ , , , – , , , , , , ], gender [ , , , , , , , , , , ], urine nitrite [ , , , , , , – , ], urine WBC [ , , , – , , ], stone diameter [ , , , , – ], diabetes mellitus [ , , , , , ], age [ , , , , ], staghorn stone [ , , , , ], mean CT value of hydronephrosis [ , ], larger stone burden [ , ], number of stones [ , ], increased irrigation rate [ , ], infectious calculi [ , ], and temperature [ , ] were valid predictors of the development of postoperative complications of urosepsis in patients with upper urinary calculi ( P < 0.05). All the forest and funnel plots are provided in Figs. (a-n). Sensitivity analysis and publication bias To assess the robustness of the study results, we conducted a sensitivity analysis exclusively on the studies included in the meta-analyses. Sensitivity analyses were performed on the altered data using a leave-one-out test to exclude studies that showed no statistical significance, indicating stable results. Funnel plot asymmetry likely resulted from study heterogeneity. The overall quality of evidence is assessed as low, particularly for primary outcomes. However, the Egger’s test yielded a value of 1.99 ( P = 0.075), suggesting no significant publication bias (Appendix A). Discussion Urolithiasis is a common disease of the urinary system. In recent years, with the development of minimally invasive technology and the updated concept of rapid rehabilitation, endoluminal lithotripsy procedures, such as ureteroscope lithotripsy (URL), retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS), and percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), have become the first-line treatment option for upper urinary calculi [ ]. Urosepsis is the most serious infection after endoluminal lithotripsy for urinary tract calculi and poses a serious threat to patient health [ ]. This systematic review summarises 25 models for predicting the risk of postoperative complications from urosepsis in patients with upper urinary calculi, with reported AUCs ranging from 0.725 to 0.992. The combined AUC after meta-analysis was 0.90 (95% CI: 0.87, 0.93), and revealed that 14 of these factors were statistically significant independent predictors. However, according to the PROBAST checklist, all studies were deemed to have a high risk of bias, limiting the practical utility of these prediction models. Furthermore, during the model evaluation, we observed inadequate reporting adherence to the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariate Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis statement in several articles. Thus, future studies should prioritize the development of new models with larger sample sizes, rigorous research designs, multicenter external validation and better transparency of reporting. Age is a critical determinant of immune function and susceptibility to sepsis. Older adults are particularly vulnerable to long-term complications from sepsis [ , ]. Thus, future studies should prioritize the development of new models with larger sample sizes, rigorous research designs, multicenter external validation and better transparency of reporting. Age is a critical determinant of immune function and susceptibility to sepsis. Older adults are particularly vulnerable to long-term complications from sepsis [ , ]. The immune system undergoes significant changes with aging, a process known as immunosenescence. This age-related decline can lead to an increased risk of infection severity and altered immune responses. studies have shown age-related declines in naive lymphocytes and an increase in CD8 + effector memory T-cells in men. In pediatric sepsis, age significantly influences the circulating immune profile. The elderly often exhibit a less robust immune response, making them more susceptible to sepsis and associated mortality. Patients with diabetes with stones increase their susceptibility to infection due to their immunosuppressive effect, making it an important predictor of postoperative urosepsis [ ]. One of the primary mechanisms contributing to immunosuppression in diabetes mellitus is chronic hyperglycemia, which directly impairs the function of immune cells. Hyperglycemia can reduce neutrophil function, decrease cytokine production, and affect macrophage activity, leading to an altered and less effective immune response [ ]. The presence of glucose in urine provides a rich environment for bacterial growth, further facilitating infection [ ]. Furthermore, temperature, as a marker of the systemic inflammatory response, holds significant value in the early detection of systemic infection postoperatively. An elevated body temperature typically indicates a widespread inflammatory or infectious response; thus, early monitoring of temperature changes postoperatively helps identify early signs of sepsis, providing a basis for timely clinical intervention [ ]. With respect to radiological features, factors such as stone diameter, number of stones, the mean CT value of hydronephrosis [ ], and stone burden [ ] demonstrated strong predictive power. Research shows that larger stones and a greater number of stones are more likely to cause prolonged obstruction of the urinary tract, leading to Elevated intrarenal pressure. Higher probability of hydronephrosis, which further compromises renal function and increases systemic inflammation [ , ]. The average CT attenuation value of the fluid in hydronephrotic kidneys is a key imaging marker for detecting infection in the urinary system. The Hounsfield Unit values derived from non-contrast CT scans can help differentiate pyonephrosis from non-pyogenic hydronephrosis. Higher HU values have been linked to the presence of infection and the increased risk of urosepsis after interventions [ ]. During endoscopic surgery, high perfusion pressure may lead to the development of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). A study retrospectively analyzed the data of 165 patients after endoscopic lithotripsy of upper urinary tract stones and found that 46 patients developed SIRS (27.88%). The incidence of SIRS in the high-pressure perfusion group was significantly higher than that in the low-pressure perfusion group [ ]. Imaging plays a crucial role in the early detection of urinary tract infections and stone-related complications, providing essential guidance for clinical management. Urine culture serves as a predictor of urinary sepsis following the presence of upper urinary tract stones [ ]. A positive urine culture indicates the presence of a urinary tract infection, which significantly increases the risk of developing urinary sepsis in the patient. Urine culture is a key diagnostic tool to identify bacterial infections in the urinary tract. In the context of upper urinary tract stones, urine cultures can help predict the risk of developing urinary sepsis, a severe complication that can arise after procedures like FURL or PCNL. A positive urine culture indicates the presence of bacteria, which, if not properly managed, can lead to sepsis [ , ]. This association is particularly strong in patients with long-term indwelling catheters or immunocompromised conditions, where the results of urine culture are crucial for assessing the risk of infection [ ]. Leukocytes and nitrites in the urine serve as biomarkers of the inflammatory response [ ], reflecting the severity of infection and the risk of complications, further enhancing their predictive value in clinical settings. Several studies have investigated the correlation between urinary leukocytes, nitrites, and urine culture results in patients suspected of having urinary tract infections [ , ]. A systematic review emphasized the functional role of urine leukocyte counts in different types of urinary tract infections [ ]. The combined presence of leukocytes and nitrites often indicates a higher likelihood of bacterial infection. An elevated white blood cell count is closely associated with bacterial urinary tract infections and sepsis onset. Nitrites, which are primarily generated by the reduction of urinary nitrates by gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli, are commonly present in the context of urinary tract infections, further indicating bacterial infection [ ]. While leukocytes and nitrites remain valuable biomarkers in the context of UTIs, ongoing research continues

The combined presence of leukocytes and nitrites often indicates a higher likelihood of bacterial infection. An elevated white blood cell count is closely associated with bacterial urinary tract infections and sepsis onset. Nitrites, which are primarily generated by the reduction of urinary nitrates by gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli, are commonly present in the context of urinary tract infections, further indicating bacterial infection [ ]. While leukocytes and nitrites remain valuable biomarkers in the context of UTIs, ongoing research continues to explore additional markers and innovative diagnostic approaches to improve the detection and management of infections and inflammatory conditions. According to the PROBAST checklist [ ], all studies exhibited a risk of bias or lacked a complete validation step. The biased results were caused mainly by the type of study design, failure to report missing values, and lack of detailed reporting of variable data analysis. Therefore, further validation of the above models is needed before their application in clinical practice. Among the included studies, 92% of the model studies were conducted in China, suggesting that urosepsis risk prediction is a high priority in China. However, research in this area remains in its initial stages, and there is a lack of recognised prediction models. We also found that for patients requiring surgical treatment, preoperative medical support tests are needed, and predictive factors included in the basic patient profile and basic laboratory tests are unavoidable, which limits the type of study design. Overall, the included models performed well, but the risk of bias remained high. Further improvements are needed for future types of studies, mainly to improve the reporting of missing values, and variable regression selection methods need to be reported in detail. Limitations This review has several limitations. First, owing to linguistic limitations, we only searched the Chinese and English literature, resulting in a small sample size and almost exclusively focusing on the Chinese population, which limits its global applicability. Second, although this review employed rigorous screening criteria for the included studies, the high risk of bias in the included studies was attributed to the heterogeneity of research designs and methodologies. Therefore, future research could broaden the search scope to include studies from non-Chinese and English-speaking countries, further investigate the impact of different research designs or methodologies on the results, and employ more appropriate statistical methods for validation. Finally, this review primarily focuses on the development and validation of models but has yet to conduct an in-depth evaluation of their effectiveness in real-world applications. Additionally, it is noteworthy that in this study, the ORs and its corresponding 95%CI were extracted from the multivariate logistic regression analysis conducted in the original studies. The observed significant heterogeneity in the results is attributed to the limitations of the original reports and the nature of the aggregated data in the meta-analysis, which did not adjust for potential confounding variables. Therefore, the analysis results should be interpreted with caution, and future individual-level studies should rigorously explore these associations and appropriately adjust for confounding factors. Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis, including 25 postoperative urosepsis risk prediction models for upper urinary calculi, summarised the characteristics of these models. The overall performance of the models was good, but there was still a high risk of bias, suggesting that health care professionals should validate and apply the models in the context of their own professional practice. In the future, the relevant risk prediction models should strictly follow the PROBAST tool to improve the research design and methodological quality in combination with clinical practice and actively perform internal and external validation to provide a universal, practical, scientific, and reasonable prediction tool for clinical practice and to prevent the occurrence of postoperative urosepsis as much as possible.
