documents.title: AUA CUA SUFU Recurrent Uncomplicated UTI in Women Guideline

chunks.content: Most women in the United States (∼60%) experience a urinary tract infection (UTI) during the course of their lifetime. Of these women, 30% to 50% risk struggling with recurrent UTIs (rUTIs), - which are defined as 2 or more UTIs within 6 months, or 3 or more UTIs within a year. Over 50% of postmenopausal (PM) women are affected by rUTIs, with an average of 2.6 episodes annually. , These infections are associated with high morbidity and often reduce quality of life, due to increased pain and related personal and professional challenges. Current clinical guidelines recommend low-dose antibiotics as a first-line approach for preventing future rUTIs. Nonetheless, because long-term exposure to antibiotics has proven to result in increased antimicrobial resistance (AMR), as well as bacterial adaptation in the urinary tract, urinary infections can last for years and become challenging to manage effectively. , As a result, scientists have sought to identify successful treatment and prophylactic strategies that do not increase the risk of AMR. Research has evidenced FDA-approved, Hiprex (methenamine hippurate), as an effective antiseptic for managing rUTIs. - For example, recently published randomized controlled trials have demonstrated noninferiority of Hiprex therapy to low-dose antibiotics in preventing rUTIs. , Hiprex has been deemed tolerable by patients, with few adverse side effects. The efficacy of Hiprex is bolstered in solutions with a lower pH, which promotes the hydrolysis of methenamine to ammonia and formaldehyde. In vitro models have suggested that when urine formaldehyde reaches specific concentrations, it can produce bacteriostatic and/or bactericidal effects. , However, clinically significant levels of urine formaldehyde have not yet been established. Moreover, Hiprex has been found to be especially potent against Escherichia coli , which is the most commonly identified bacterial species in urine cultures (UCs) from women with rUTIs, , but less is known about its effect on other strains. Thus, we sought to determine the average urine pH in PM women affected by rUTIs, such that we could better comprehend the role of Hiprex as an antibiotic-sparing agent for long-term rUTI prophylaxis in that population. We also sought to investigate urinary pH levels in relationship to varying bacterial species in positive UC. Our group hypothesized that urinary pH levels may differ between women with current rUTIs or a history of UTIs and those that do not have a history of UTIs. METHODS Following Internal Review Board approval (STU 08210-016), a large, prospective database of non-neurogenic PM women with uncomplicated rUTI from a tertiary care center specializing in rUTI management was reviewed for concurrent data on urine pH through urinalysis and UC in the outpatient clinical setting. UTI in women with a history of uncomplicated rUTI was defined based on established UTI urinary symptoms and associated urinalysis and UC confirming a bacterial infection of the bladder. “Uncomplicated” meant the infection was present in the absence of mechanistic or structural abnormalities or comorbidities causing rUTI. Three groups were analyzed: PM women with no history of UTI and PM women with a history of rUTI, either with no current UTI based on negative UC, or with current UTI confirmed by UC. PM women with no history of UTI served as the control group and their data originated from an NIH study (#1R01DK131267-01) during which urine pH was measured longitudinally (up to 4 times over the course of 3 months). Midstream urine specimens were collected into sterile containers for urinalysis and UC. On receipt, urine pH was evaluated using institutional standard operating procedures for urinalysis as described by the Siemens CLINITEK Novus protocol for the UN3000 Urine Chemistry Analyzer. UCs were labeled and assessed for specimen condition. The samples were processed, inoculated, incubated, and analyzed for bacterial growth, as described using standard operating procedures (Supplementary Appendix A, http://links.lww.com/JU9/A170 ). Bacterial species were identified using matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization–time-of-flight tests, and an antimicrobial susceptibility test by Microscan was conducted to identify growth. The data—including organism identification and susceptibility—were reported. Electronic medical records (EPIC) were used to tally the information on urinalysis and UC. Descriptive statistics were provided as medians and IQR for continuous measures and as frequencies and percentages for categorical measures. The median urine pH per patient was calculated for each group, and a χ 2 test analyzed association between a median pH of 6 or less by group. Mixed-model analysis was also used to determine if there was a difference in urine pH between the 3 groups, using a compound symmetric covariance structure to account for the multiple urine pH measurements per patient. For the patients with current UTI, we used stacked bar charts to visualize the urine pH by bacterial species. All analyses were completed at the 0.05 significance level using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc). The NIH (grant 1R01DK131267-01) compensated those in the “never had a UTI” group. Mixed-model analysis was also used to determine if there was a difference in urine pH between the 3 groups, using a compound symmetric covariance structure to account for the multiple urine pH measurements per patient. For the patients with current UTI, we used stacked bar charts to visualize the urine pH by bacterial species. All analyses were completed at the 0.05 significance level using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc). The NIH (grant 1R01DK131267-01) compensated those in the “never had a UTI” group. RESULTS From 2001 to 2025, the database yielded a total of 1669 UCs with associated pH measurements to be considered for the analysis. Of those, 375 UCs were excluded because they came from women < 55 years, and 18 UCs were excluded for possible contaminants. The final study population included a total of 1276 UCs from 345 PM women, with a median age of 70 years, and a median of 3 UCs. Patient demographics are presented in Table. UC and pH For those with a current UTI when the UC was obtained, the overall median pH was found to be 6 (IQR: 5.5-6; Figure ). The cultures from individuals with a history of rUTI, but no current UTI, yielded a median pH of 6 (IQR: 5.5-6), while cultures obtained from those with an active UTI had a median pH of 6 (IQR: 5.5-6.8). The patients who never had a UTI had a slightly higher urine pH than PM women with a current UTI (0.051) or those with a history of UTI but no current UTI (0.12), although not significantly so. The rate of median urine pH ≤ 6 was 76% (94/123) when individuals had a current UTI and 77% (255/332) when participants had a history of rUTI but no current UTI. Interestingly, only 65% (17/26) of women with no UTI history had a urine pH ≤ 6, but this was not a significant difference compared with the others (χ 2 P = .4; Figure ). Bacterial Species E. coli was the most commonly identified bacterial species in UCs (n = 133 cultures from 81 patients), followed by Klebsiella (n = 46 cultures from 36 patients), Enterococcus faecalis (n = 31 cultures from 25 patients), Proteus (n = 16 cultures from 14 patients), and Gram-negative rods (n = 12 cultures from 10 patients). Of patients in whom E. coli was present, 78% of patients had a median pH value ≤ 6. This trend was observed across many of the bacterial species, where a majority were identified in cultures with a pH of ≤ 6. Minimal association was noted between low pH and bacterial species (Figure ). DISCUSSION To the best of our knowledge, this is the first controlled study comparing urine pH among 3 groups of PM women, namely, those who had an uncomplicated history of rUTI with a current UTI or not, and those who never experienced a UTI. Our findings revealed that roughly three-quarters of PM women with a current UTI or those not infected at the time of the UC, but with a history of rUTIs, had a urinary pH around or below 6, while only about a half of PM women who never had a UTI yielded urinary pH levels of ≤ 6. Urine pH affects the efficacy with which antiseptic, Hiprex, is capable of hydrolyzing to ammonia and formaldehyde, which exert bactericidal and/or bacteriostatic effects on UTI-causing bacteria. Prior research has indicated that methenamine hippurate may be associated with decreased UTI frequency for up to 1 year. , , However, given that the efficacy of Hiprex as an antiseptic relies largely on a lower pH environment, the question addressed by this study was: how many women in the affected population could potentially benefit from well-tolerated Hiprex as a prophylactic approach? To date, a paucity of research has focused on urinary pH in the context of rUTIs, particularly in PM women. It is essential to better understand urinary pH among this disproportionately affected population such that therapeutic strategies influenced by pH can be considered for appropriate patient selection and treatment optimization. Since Hiprex converts to bactericidal formaldehyde more effectively in a lower urinary pH, this therapy may be further bolstered when administered with agents that acidify the urine, such as hippuric acid, a constituent of Hiprex, or vitamin C. , However, the degree of additional acidification achieved by these products is modest. In fact, it is very difficult to increase urinary acidification. this therapy may be further bolstered when administered with agents that acidify the urine, such as hippuric acid, a constituent of Hiprex, or vitamin C. , However, the degree of additional acidification achieved by these products is modest. In fact, it is very difficult to increase urinary acidification. Our group has studied 3-day urine pH and food diaries (Supplementary Appendix B, http://links.lww.com/JU9/A170 ) in PM women with rUTI to determine if certain foods can increase or decrease urine pH. , Most patients were found to have fairly tightly regulated urinary pH levels either constantly in the low (pH < 6) ranges or in the high ranges, regardless of their food and/or fluid intake. Only a few were noted to experience low to high urinary pH fluctuations over time. Nonetheless, this simple home-based evaluation with urinary dipsticks can prove useful for selecting those with a low urinary pH before embarking on a long-term Hiprex therapy. Some conditions may affect urine pH and/or the effectiveness of a therapy such as Hiprex. Diabetes mellitus (DM), for example, heightens the risk of UTIs (and is associated with increased severity and worse outcomes), due to impaired immune function and elevated sugar levels in the urine, which can enhance bacterial growth. However, regardless of dietary factors, body size, or age, urine pH is often more acidic in the context of DM, , suggesting that this subpopulation may be of particular interest for targeting with antibiotic-sparing Hiprex as a prophylaxis strategy that does not increase the risk of AMR. Such therapeutic strategies may become increasingly important in the context of the rising incidence of DM, and the data suggesting this population have a higher risk of UTI. This study benefited from a prospective tracking of a series of PM women with uncomplicated rUTI from a database which collected urinary symptoms of UTI and urinalysis and UCs concomitantly with the same clinical provider in a specialized tertiary center. The modalities of urine collection and analyses along with reporting did not change over time. This study was limited by the inability to generalize, since these data originated from a single center and comprised a mostly Caucasian population. In addition, some patients may have had UCs obtained outside of our center and not available for retrieval in EPIC. Finally, hormone and estrogen status were unknown, and the link between estrogen and urine pH should be investigated in future work. CONCLUSION In this long-term prospective database study, three-quarters of PM women with a history of uncomplicated rUTI, whether infected or not, presented with urine pH of 6 or less. More than half of women with no history of UTI fell in that same category. Understanding urine pH is important for determining long-term preventive rUTI opportunities, especially when Hiprex is considered due to its unique mechanism of action which demands an acidic urinary environment. In addition, research has demonstrated that Hiprex is most effective against E. coli , enterococci, and staphylococci, which, in the population of PM women studied here, were commonly present. ETHICS STATEMENT Following Internal Review Board approval (STU 08210-016), a large, prospective database of non-neurogenic PM women with uncomplicated rUTI from a tertiary care center specializing in rUTI management was reviewed for concurrent data on urine pH via urinalysis and UC in the outpatient clinical setting. documents.title: AUA Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Interstitial Cystitis Bladder Pain Syndrome

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is a chronic, debilitating condition characterized by pelvic pain, bladder discomfort, and urinary symptoms in the absence of other identifiable causes [ ]. Despite significant advancements in understanding IC/BPS, accurate diagnosis remains challenging due to its multifactorial nature and symptom overlap with other lower urinary tract disorders [ , ]. Several validated questionnaires have been developed to improve diagnostic standardization. For example, the O’Leary-Sant Interstitial Cystitis Symptom and Problem Index (ICSI/ICPI) is a comprehensive tool, with a score of ≥12 yielding sensitivity of 86% and specificity of 65% [ ]. However, it lacks precision and remains dependent on subjective patient reporting. The visual analog scale (VAS) for bladder pain, while simpler and more practical (VAS score ≥7: diagnostic accuracy = 0.94, positive predictive value [PPV] = 0.82, negative predictive value [NPV] = 0.97), is also limited by individual variability in pain perception and becomes less reliable in patients with scores below 7 [ ]. As a result, although these tools offer partial improvements in diagnostic consistency, their reliance on subjective symptomatology limits overall accuracy and contributes to the typical diagnostic delay. The current diagnostic approach continues to depend largely on patient-reported symptoms, cystoscopic findings, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses—factors that often delay treatment initiation and impact patient outcomes negatively [ ]. Recent research has focused on the identification of objective biomarkers that could provide more reliable and noninvasive diagnostic options for IC/BPS [ , ]. Inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, neurogenic growth factor–related markers, and oxidative stress markers in urine have emerged as promising candidates due to their involvement in the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying IC/BPS [ ]. Additionally, patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and voiding diary data may have the potential to provide valuable clinical parameters to further support diagnosis [ , ]. However, individual biomarkers alone have shown limited sensitivity and specificity [ , ], suggesting that a comprehensive, integrative approach incorporating both urinary biomarkers and clinical parameters (including PROs and information from voiding diary) could enhance diagnostic accuracy. Accordingly, the present study (1) compares existing symptom-based diagnostic tools with biomarker-based approaches, and (2) develops and validates a multivariable diagnostic prediction model integrating urinary biomarkers with clinical parameters, to enhance diagnostic performance for IC/BPS. 2 Patients and methods 2.1 Study population and diagnostic definition This study follows the principles of multivariable diagnostic prediction model development, and the reporting adheres to the TRIPOD guidelines where applicable. As a retrospective study utilizing existing biospecimens and clinical data, no formal prospective study registration or protocol identifier was applicable. This retrospective study ultimately included 385 participants: 344 patients with clinically confirmed IC/BPS and 41 non-IC/BPS controls. A detailed breakdown of the patient selection process is presented in . Participants were identified from an institutional database consisting of patients evaluated for IC/BPS at Hualien Tzu Chi Hospital. The inclusion criteria were the following: 1. Availability of midstream urine samples collected prior to cystoscopic hydrodistension 2. Completion of cystoscopic hydrodistension and videourodynamic studies 3. Absence of active urinary tract infection at the time of evaluation IC/BPS diagnoses were established according to the European Association of Urology guidelines, defined as pain, pressure, or discomfort perceived to be related to the urinary bladder, accompanied by at least one additional symptom such as increased daytime and/or night-time urinary frequency [ ]. Confusable conditions were excluded based on the criteria outlined by the European Society for the Study of Interstitial Cystitis (ESSIC) [ , , ]. To ensure diagnostic consistency and enable phenotypic characterization, all participants underwent standardized cystoscopic hydrodistension under anesthesia and videourodynamic studies [ ]. The diagnosis of IC/BPS was further supported by cystoscopic findings in accordance with the Asian guidelines [ ], which emphasize the presence and grading of glomerulations following hydrodistension as the diagnostic criteria. Patients with normal cystoscopic findings after hydrodistension were excluded from the IC/BPS cohort. IC/BPS diagnosis was based on the ESSIC and Asian clinical practice guidelines, which include cystoscopic hydrodistension findings and are routinely used in our institution. This approach was preferred to the American Urological Association (AUA) guidelines [ ], which are applied less commonly in our local context. 2.2 Control phenotype Control participants were individuals presenting with lower urinary tract symptoms but without bladder or pelvic pain. They were stringently screened to exclude any identifiable lower urinary tract dysfunction, as confirmed by videourodynamic studies, including detrusor overactivity, bladder outlet obstruction, dysfunctional voiding, or neurogenic bladder. Additionally, participants with active urinary tract infections at the time of enrollment were excluded. All participants had previously been enrolled in our institutional review board–approved clinical studies focused on IC/BPS (approval no. 113-151-B), and urine samples were collected with prior informed consent [ ]. Given the retrospective nature of the current study and the prior consent for a biomarker analysis, the requirement for additional informed consent was formally waived. 2.3 Clinical

Additionally, participants with active urinary tract infections at the time of enrollment were excluded. All participants had previously been enrolled in our institutional review board–approved clinical studies focused on IC/BPS (approval no. 113-151-B), and urine samples were collected with prior informed consent [ ]. Given the retrospective nature of the current study and the prior consent for a biomarker analysis, the requirement for additional informed consent was formally waived. 2.3 Clinical parameters Two key clinical parameters were incorporated into the diagnostic model. Bladder pain severity was assessed using a standardized VAS, ranging from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst imaginable pain) [ ]. Functional bladder capacity (FBC) was defined as the maximum voided volume recorded over a continuous 3-d period using a detailed patient-completed voiding diary [ ]. These parameters were selected based on their established clinical relevance in reflecting symptom burden and bladder function in IC/BPS patients [ , ]. Both pain scores and 3-d bladder diaries were collected at the initial patient evaluation visit, prior to urine biomarker sample collection and cystoscopic hydrodistension. 2.4 Urine biomarkers All biomarker measurements were performed in a blinded fashion, without any knowledge of the participants’ clinical diagnosis. Urine samples were collected immediately prior to cystoscopic hydrodistension, ensuring minimal delay between biomarker sampling and diagnostic confirmation. Midstream urine samples (50 ml) were obtained via spontaneous voiding at full bladder capacity, prior to cystoscopic hydrodistension. Immediately after collection, samples were placed on ice and centrifuged at 1800 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was aliquoted and stored at –80 °C. Prior to the biomarker analysis, samples were thawed on ice and centrifuged again at 12 000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C to ensure removal of cellular debris [ ]. Urinary biomarkers were quantified using multiplex bead-based immunoassays and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) [ ]. Proinflammatory and regulatory cytokines/chemokines—including interleukin (IL)-8; C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 10; monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1); eotaxin; IL-6; macrophage inflammatory protein-1β; regulated on activation, normal T-cell expressed and secreted; tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α); brain-derived neurotrophic factor; and total antioxidant capacity—were measured using the Milliplex Human Cytokine/Chemokine Magnetic Bead Panel (Millipore, Darmstadt, Germany). Oxidative stress biomarkers, including 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) and 8-isoprostane, were measured using commercially available ELISA kits (K4160-100; Biovision, and DI-900-010; Enzo Life Sciences). Levels of 8-isoprostane were normalized to urinary creatinine concentration using a creatinine assay kit (ADI-907-030A; Enzo Life Sciences). Biomarker concentrations were calculated based on median fluorescence intensity or optical density in accordance with the manufacturers’ protocols. No adverse events were reported during urine collection or cystoscopic hydrodistension. 2.5 Statistical analysis All included participants ( n = 385) had complete biomarker and clinical data, allowing for a complete-case analysis. All statistical analyses were conducted using deidentified data, independent of clinical label information. We developed and internally validated a multivariable diagnostic prediction model using logistic regression with stepwise forward selection to identify the most discriminative combination of urinary biomarkers and clinical parameters. All candidate variables, including urinary biomarkers, FBC, and VAS pain scores (0–10 scale), were treated as continuous variables in the model. No categorization, binarization, or thresholding was performed. The full dataset was split randomly into a training cohort (70%) and a testing cohort (30%). Biomarkers and clinical parameters with a low discriminative ability in a univariate analysis (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] <0.6) were excluded from multivariable modeling. No formal sample size calculation was conducted, as this was a retrospective study using all available eligible data. Model construction was performed exclusively within the training cohort. The final models were then validated independently in the testing cohort to assess generalizability. The classification threshold for sensitivity and specificity was selected using Youden’s index based on the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve in the training set. These thresholds were derived for internal validation purposes and are not intended as clinically validated cutoffs. Diagnostic performance metrics included AUROC, overall accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and R version 4.x (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). 3 Results Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics, as well as urinary biomarker distributions, were comparable between the training cohort ( n = 269, 69.9%) and the testing cohort ( n = 116, 30.1%), with no statistically significant differences observed across key variables ( ). This comparability minimized baseline confounding and validated the reliability of subsequent model training and evaluation. In the training dataset, the diagnostic utility of each urinary biomarker was assessed via an ROC curve analysis ( ). Among all individually tested biomarkers, urinary 8-OHdG exhibited the highest discriminative power for identifying

This comparability minimized baseline confounding and validated the reliability of subsequent model training and evaluation. In the training dataset, the diagnostic utility of each urinary biomarker was assessed via an ROC curve analysis ( ). Among all individually tested biomarkers, urinary 8-OHdG exhibited the highest discriminative power for identifying IC/BPS, with an AUROC of 0.838 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.783–0.894). Other biomarkers also demonstrated statistically significant but lower discriminative performance, including TNF-α (AUROC = 0.769), MCP-1 (AUROC = 0.710), 8-isoprostane (AUROC = 0.704), and eotaxin (AUROC = 0.656); all were statistically significant, with p values of <0.001 except for eotaxin ( p = 0.006; ). The specific AUROC values, 95% CIs, and p values for each biomarker are detailed in the legend. Biomarkers with AUROC values above 0.60 were retained for multivariate model development. A two-marker model comprising 8-OHdG and TNF-α yielded excellent diagnostic performance, with AUROC values of 0.958 in the training set and 0.952 in the test set, demonstrating robust internal consistency ( ). To further refine the model, clinical parameters were incorporated. The addition of patient-reported bladder pain severity, assessed via the VAS, improved diagnostic performance markedly. The final integrative model, which included 8-OHdG, TNF-α, and VAS, achieved an AUROC of 0.997 in the training cohort and 0.997 in the testing cohort ( ). This model demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy (95.7%), sensitivity (96.2%), and specificity (91.7%), highlighting its potential as a noninvasive, high-performing diagnostic tool for IC/BPS applicable in real-world clinical settings. 4 Discussion This study presents the development and internal validation of a multivariable diagnostic prediction model for IC/BPS, integrating both urinary biomarkers and clinical parameters. Our modeling approach follows the established frameworks for diagnostic prediction research, rather than classical diagnostic test accuracy studies. We identified several novel and important findings: (1) the integrative model combining urinary 8-OHdG, TNF-α, and VAS score yielded the highest diagnostic performance; (2) among models based solely on urinary biomarkers, the combination of 8-OHdG and TNF-α demonstrated the strongest performance; and (3) if limited to a single urinary biomarker, 8-OHdG outperformed other inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, and neurogenic markers in diagnostic accuracy. Compared with our previous study [ ], which focused solely on clusters of urinary biomarkers for the identification of IC/BPS and its subtypes, the current work represents a significant advance by integrating both key urinary biomarkers and clinically relevant parameters (pain score and FBC) into a single diagnostic model. This integrated approach resulted in superior diagnostic performance and greater potential for practical clinical application. Although single biomarker strategies are attractive due to their cost effectiveness and simplicity, these often fail to differentiate IC/BPS from other overlapping urological conditions [ ]. Our integrative model overcomes this limitation by combining objective biochemical signals with clinically relevant symptom assessments, achieving superior diagnostic discrimination. Oxidative stress is a well-established contributor to IC/BPS pathology [ , , , , ]. The consistent diagnostic performance of 8-OHdG, a robust marker of oxidative DNA damage, highlights its potential role as a core biomarker in clinical diagnosis [ ]. Although previous studies have suggested its involvement in IC/BPS, few have successfully embedded it into a validated diagnostic algorithm. Our findings reaffirm the relevance of oxidative stress and support the clinical applicability of 8-OHdG. The inclusion of TNF-α, a proinflammatory cytokine involved in IC/BPS-related inflammation [ , ], improved model performance further. The established role of TNF-α in inflammation, immune activation, and bladder pain mechanisms enhances the biological rationale for its inclusion [ , , ]. The dual-biomarker model (8-OHdG + TNF-α) alone achieved an AUROC of 0.96 in the training cohort and 0.95 in the testing cohort, offering an optimal balance of sensitivity and specificity for purely biomarker-based screening. Crucially, the integration of patient-reported bladder pain severity via the VAS elevated model performance to near-perfect levels (AUROC = 0.997 in the training and 0.997 in the testing cohort). This reflects the clinical reality that symptom severity often correlates with underlying pathophysiological changes. While VAS is subjective and categorized as a PRO, our data also demonstrate that substitution of VAS with a purely objective clinical parameter such as FBC—when combined with 8-OHdG and TNF-α—still yielded strong diagnostic accuracy (AUROC = 0.947, accuracy = 96.6%, sensitivity = 98.1%, and specificity = 83.3%). Thus, clinicians may flexibly tailor the diagnostic model based on available resources and patient preferences. Importantly, the robustness of our model was confirmed through consistent results in independent training and testing subsets, supporting its generalizability across clinical environments. Thus, clinicians may flexibly tailor the diagnostic model based on available resources and patient preferences. Importantly, the robustness of our model was confirmed through consistent results in independent training and testing subsets, supporting its generalizability across clinical environments. The model’s high specificity is especially valuable for IC/BPS, where misdiagnosis often leads to delayed and inappropriate treatments. Clinically, this model has several advantages: it is entirely noninvasive, relies on standard and scalable assays, and incorporates straightforward clinical metrics. Compared with validated questionnaires such as the ICSI/ICPI (AUROC = 0.85), or the Pain, Urgency, Frequency Symptom Scale (AUROC = 0.92) [ , ], our model demonstrated significantly greater discriminative power (AUROC = 1.00), with greater PPV and NPV. These attributes make it feasible for use in outpatient and telemedicine settings. Given the economic burden associated with testing multiple biomarkers, our model also provides guidance for cost-effective decision-making—offering clinicians high-performance options based on one, two, or three variables. Moreover, the implications of our model may extend beyond diagnosis. Both 8-OHdG and TNF-α are implicated in chronic disease progression and may serve as prognostic markers in IC/BPS. Future studies could investigate whether longitudinal monitoring of these markers provides actionable insight into disease trajectory or therapeutic responsiveness. Despite these strengths, certain limitations must be acknowledged. Variables such as diet, medication use, or comorbidities may influence urinary biomarker levels. Although age and the prevalence of hypertension were not significantly different between groups in our study, both factors may affect oxidative stress and could confound urinary biomarker measurements [ , ]. The absence of histological data also limits correlation with tissue-level pathology. Imbalances in sex and age in our study may have introduced a bias and limited generalizability; a meaningful sex-specific analysis was not possible due to the small number of male cases. Future studies with a more balanced sex distribution, age-matched groups, and larger male cohorts are needed to validate our findings and assess sex-specific diagnostic performance. Although the AUA guidelines do not recommend routine cystoscopy, hydrodistension, or urodynamic studies for the diagnosis of IC/BPS [ ], all patients in our study underwent standardized cystoscopic hydrodistension and videourodynamic assessments to enhance diagnostic precision. This rigorous diagnostic approach was primarily based on Asian guidelines, which emphasize the importance of cystoscopy or hydrodistension as an essential component for the definitive diagnosis of IC/BPS [ ]. By adopting this approach, we aimed to ensure a homogeneous disease cohort and minimize the misclassification bias during biomarker model development. While this strategy strengthens the internal validity of our findings, it may limit their generalizability to broader clinical settings where less invasive diagnostic criteria, such as those recommended by the AUA, are applied. Future studies should evaluate the performance of our biomarker model in more diverse populations diagnosed under varying international standards. Additionally, the small number of patients with Hunner lesions in our cohort limited the feasibility of a meaningful subgroup analysis. Larger and more heterogeneous samples will be necessary to validate the model across IC/BPS subtypes and to assess its applicability in distinguishing IC/BPS from other pelvic pain syndromes. As a single-center retrospective study, a selection bias cannot be excluded, which may limit generalizability. Since only patients who underwent cystoscopic hydrodistension and videourodynamic studies were included, an ascertainment bias is possible, as this cohort may not represent the broader IC/BPS population. This study used a single random 70/30 split-sample internal validation strategy, which may yield an overly optimistic estimate of model performance due to sampling variability. The high AUROC values may reflect dataset-specific patterns rather than true generalizability, and optimism-corrected estimates should be considered in future work. More robust internal validation methods, such as cross-validation or bootstrapping, should be applied in future studies. The use of stepwise logistic regression for model construction may also increase the risk of overfitting and result in unstable models. Penalized regression techniques (eg, Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator, ridge, or elastic net) may offer greater robustness and should be considered in future model development. Stepwise selection was used due to the exploratory nature of this retrospective study, but we acknowledge its limitations. Furthermore, calibration assessments such as calibration plots or Brier scores were not performed, limiting the ability to evaluate the agreement between predicted and observed probabilities. The classification thresholds used to calculate sensitivity and specificity were derived from ROC curves using Youden’s index within the training dataset. Stepwise selection was used due to the exploratory nature of this retrospective study, but we acknowledge its limitations. Furthermore, calibration assessments such as calibration plots or Brier scores were not performed, limiting the ability to evaluate the agreement between predicted and observed probabilities. The classification thresholds used to calculate sensitivity and specificity were derived from ROC curves using Youden’s index within the training dataset. These thresholds are data driven and may be prone to overfitting; therefore, these are intended solely for internal evaluation and are not proposed as clinically validated cutoffs. Additionally, the PPV of our biomarker panel was evaluated in a retrospectively identified cohort with established diagnoses, rather than in newly presenting, undiagnosed patients. The lack of a priori sample size calculation represents a limitation and may affect statistical power estimation. Prospective multicenter studies enrolling patients based on clinical suspicion and evaluating model performance against the final clinical diagnosis in real-world settings are needed to validate the panel’s predictive performance and to confirm its true clinical utility and generalizability. Only internal validation using a random split-sample method was performed. Although this provides initial support for model performance, external validation in independent and multicenter cohorts is necessary to confirm generalizability. While this study focuses primarily on the development of a noninvasive diagnostic model for IC/BPS, it does not address treatment response or prognostic prediction. As the urine samples and clinical data were collected prior to therapeutic interventions, we were not able to assess whether the identified biomarkers can discriminate between responders and nonresponders. We fully acknowledge this limitation, and future prospective studies incorporating longitudinal follow-up are warranted to determine the discriminant validity of these biomarkers in monitoring treatment outcomes. Additionally, future work should explore additional biomarkers such as serum or stool-based indicators [ , ], and integrate the model into clinical decision support tools. Sympathetic nervous system assessment may also represent a promising direction for objective biomarkers in future research [ , , , ]. Furthermore, incorporation of machine learning frameworks and mobile health platforms may enhance the model’s scalability and utility. Finally, creatinine normalization for urinary 8-OHdG, although used widely, remains controversial for bladder-derived biomarkers due to potential variability from inflammation. Alternative normalization strategies, including the use of bladder-specific markers such as hyaluronic acid, might be considered in future research [ ]. The proposed integrative diagnostic model has the potential to improve clinical care by providing a noninvasive tool that complements existing clinical evaluation. In practice, this model could support earlier identification of IC/BPS, especially in settings where cystoscopic hydrodistension is not feasible or available. By reducing dependence on invasive procedures, the model may streamline diagnostic workflows and reduce patient burden. Nonetheless, we recognize the potential risks of false positives or negatives, which could lead to over- or undertreatment. Therefore, external validation and prospective studies are essential to evaluate the clinical consequences, including impacts on diagnostic accuracy, treatment decision-making, and patient outcomes. In summary, this discussion underscores the biological significance, clinical relevance, and translational potential of an integrative diagnostic strategy for IC/BPS. By combining urinary 8-OHdG, TNF-α, and symptom-based metrics, we offer a high-performance, accessible tool that bridges molecular diagnostics and patient-centered care. 5 Conclusions We developed and internally validated a clinically actionable diagnostic model for IC/BPS that integrates urinary 8-OHdG, TNF-α, and patient-reported pain scores. This model demonstrated strong diagnostic performance in both the training and the testing cohort, indicating potential clinical utility. Our findings reinforce the value of combining biological data with clinical insights to improve the accuracy and efficiency of IC/BPS diagnosis. By reducing reliance on subjective reporting, this approach may help address diagnostic delays and facilitate more timely, appropriate treatment. However, further prospective and multicenter validation is required before clinical implementation. With such additional evidence, this model may ultimately contribute to advancing precision diagnostics in urology and improving care for patients with chronic bladder pain. documents.title: AUA Evaluation and Treatment of Cryptorchidism Guideline

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Non‐scrotal testis (NST) is the most common congenital abnormality among boys, with a prevalence of 1%–8% among newborns [ , ]. The prevalence is even higher among boys born prematurely or small for gestational age. Many NSTs descend after birth, but spontaneous descent is unlikely to occur after 6 months [ , , ]. At the age of 1 year, 1% of boys still has non‐scrotal testes [ ], yielding an incidence of NST of 20.000 per year in the European Union. If treatment is not performed timely, boys with NST have an increased risk of subfertility [ , ] and neoplasia [ , ]. Therefore, surgical correction before the age of 18 months is the current standard of care [ , , , ]. Previous studies reporting results after orchidopexy have been limited by levels of loss to follow‐up ranging between 15% and 22% [ , , ]. Such a large portion of patients might introduce selection bias. In a prior evaluation of boys operated for NST in our center, we observed a similar rate of loss to follow‐up. Henceforth, a concerted effort was made to achieve near‐complete levels of follow‐up of patients (aim: follow‐up rate of > 95%). According to literature, the overall success rate of all orchidopexies (palpable and non‐palpable testes) is at least 88%, and 92% for inguinal orchidopexies (palpable testes) [ , ]. Unsuccessful surgery may result in an incorrect position of the testis or testicular atrophy. We postulated that the surgeon's level of training might affect the outcome of orchidopexies. For these reasons, we retrospectively reviewed all patients operated consecutively for NST at our institution over a period of 2 years. Goal of our study was to assess short‐term complication rates and postoperative outcomes of orchidopexies in a patient cohort with very low percentage of loss to follow‐up. 2 Methods Data on all patients aged < 18 years who underwent orchidopexy at the pediatric urology department at Wilhelmina's Children Hospital UMC Utrecht, a tertiary care center, between January 2015 and December 2016 were analyzed retrospectively. Children with pre‐existent testicular atrophy and/or syndromic disorders were excluded. The latter to create a group as homogeneous as possible with less chance of intrinsic testicular tissue dysfunction. The results of three surgical procedures for non‐scrotal testes were evaluated: firstly, inguinal orchidopexy for inguinal localized testes; secondly, laparoscopic (staged) Fowler‐Stephens procedures for high abdominal testes; and thirdly, redo cases. The indication for redo cases was a non‐scrotal position after surgery; in most cases, referred from a general hospital. All surgeries were performed or supervised by 2‐year fellowship‐trained pediatric urologists (FEAPU). Key points of the surgical techniques used are summarized in Table . The standardized surgical steps were combined with careful tissue handling. All patients were reviewed at the outpatient clinic 6 months after surgery. In case of a no‐show, patients and parents were actively contacted to attend a rescheduled follow‐up visit. Success was defined as the scrotal position of the testis with no signs of testicular atrophy upon clinical examination. Testicular units were classified as atrophic when they were significantly smaller (typically ≥ 50% reduction in size compared to the contralateral testis) and exhibited either a soft consistency or a characteristically firm consistency, in combination with a small size (generally < 1–2 mL, depending on age). Complications were ranked according to the Clavien‐Dindo classification [ ]. The institutional ethics committee approved the study and data extraction from patient records (ABR‐47524). 3 Results A total of 254 orchidopexies were performed in 211 patients. Five patients, constituting 2% (5/254) of testicular units, were lost to follow‐up due to relocation abroad. Follow‐up rate was thus 98% (Table ). Short‐term complications were wound infections (4/249) and, in one case, injury of the vas deferens. The short‐term complication rate was calculated as 5/249 (2%). Table gives an overview of short‐term complications stratified by type of surgery and complication grade according to the Clavien‐Dindo classification. One patient developed necrotizing fasciitis due to a streptococcal infection following an inguinal orchidopexy (classified as a grade IV complication). This rare complication was successfully treated with immediate surgery and admission to the intensive care. In the end, testicular volume was adequate, but the testicle was located in the inguinal canal. Median follow‐up was 7 months (interquartile range: 5–9 months) after the last operative procedure. Outcome was deemed satisfactory in 237/249 (95%) testicular units operated. Outcome at follow‐up per operative procedure is presented in Table . In four cases, the position of the testis was inguinal; 3 after inguinal orchidopexy and 1 following a laparoscopic staged Fowler Stephens procedure (which was ascribed to insufficient length of the testicular vessels). In total 8 (3.2%) testicular units were atrophied. 4 Discussion In conclusion, in this single‐center, retrospective analysis of 249 orchidopexies, all performed under the supervision of or by fellowship‐trained

the inguinal canal. Median follow‐up was 7 months (interquartile range: 5–9 months) after the last operative procedure. Outcome was deemed satisfactory in 237/249 (95%) testicular units operated. Outcome at follow‐up per operative procedure is presented in Table . In four cases, the position of the testis was inguinal; 3 after inguinal orchidopexy and 1 following a laparoscopic staged Fowler Stephens procedure (which was ascribed to insufficient length of the testicular vessels). In total 8 (3.2%) testicular units were atrophied. 4 Discussion In conclusion, in this single‐center, retrospective analysis of 249 orchidopexies, all performed under the supervision of or by fellowship‐trained pediatric urologists, the overall success rate was 95%. Short‐term complications consisted mostly of post‐operative infections and occurred in 2% of procedures. Loss to follow‐up in our study was minimalized by aggressively managing no‐shows at the outpatient, to no more than 2%. The reported outcomes can, therefore, be used in more accurate patient/parental counseling in daily clinical practice and clinical guidelines. As of now, three randomized control trials of (the different surgical approaches to) orchidopexy have been published [ , , ]. The vast majority of studies reporting on orchidopexy outcomes have predominantly been retrospective analyses of single‐center cohorts. In 2022, the American Pediatric Surgical Association published a systematic literature review concerning orchidopexy surgery outcome [ ]. In the final analysis, the authors included 260 articles on a total of 5035 orchidopexies combined. The median participant number of these studies was 120 [ , , ]. In short, the long‐term outcome of orchidopexies depends on the preoperative position of the NST (inguinal vs. abdominal), the procedure performed (open vs. laparoscopic) and whether the NST has been operated on previously (first attempt, staged vs. redo‐orchidopexy). In our study, the success rate of all procedures combined was 95%. Procedures were deemed unsuccessful either due to atrophy or inadequate position (i.e., inguinal and not scrotal) of the operated testicle upon follow‐up. In two‐thirds of failed procedures (or 3.2% of all procedures) the outcome was deemed unsatisfactory due to atrophy. In literature, testicular atrophy following orchidopexy has been reported to range from 0% to 9% [ , , ]. Inadequate position of the operated testicle upon follow‐up was the outcome in one‐third of unsuccessful procedures (1.6% of all procedures). With regard to inguinal position following orchidopexy, literature states an average rate of 1.3% for inguinal orchidopexy and a range of 1.5%–5% for orchidopexy in abdominally located testes [ ]. Outcomes in our study, 1.2% and 4% respectively, were within these expectations. Finally, short‐term complications in our cohort were mostly of infectious nature. Infectious complications following orchidopexy surgery reported in literature have varied between 1% and 3% [ , ]. The 2% complication rate in our study compares well with these findings. In our cohort, outcomes were within known ranges when compared with success and complication rates previously reported in literature [ , , ]. Most notably, our redo operation rates (8.5%) are comparable to recent cohorts (9.3%), which is an improvement compared to older cohorts (15%) [ ]. This improved outcome over the years might be due to increased specialty training. In the future, outcomes might further be improved by honing existing techniques or even transitioning into others, such as single incision scrotal orchiopexy or staged traction orchiopexy [ , , , , ]. Like previous studies into orchidopexy outcomes, ours was a retrospective analysis of a single center cohort. However, it stands out by its very high follow‐up rate of no less than 98%. Loss to follow‐up occurred only due to patients relocating to another country. This minimal loss allowed us to ascertain the actual complication rate of orchidopexy surgery, minimize bias, and thus improve the reliability of outcomes reported. These data can, in turn, be used both to inform patients and their parents and to improve clinical practice guidelines. Indeed, a recent report identified the lack of complete follow‐up data as a barrier to implementation and a possible area for improvement specifically of interest to guidelines on NST [ ]. Our study has several limitations. One is its retrospective character, which can introduce bias and should be taken into account when considering the validity of the data. Second, data were obtained from a single surgical center, which may limit the generalizability of the results. Also, albeit that our study cohort size was well above the median number of patients in previous studies, attaining higher patient numbers would have allowed us to assess complication rates and outcomes better, especially within surgical technique subgroups and specifically within the staged orchidopexy group, which holds only 25 testicular units in 18 patients. Finally, our study reported on both inguinal orchidopexy and abdominal orchidopexy procedures combined, whereas most studies have reported on one treatment strategy only. We did, however, present outcomes for both procedures separately. It is our

Also, albeit that our study cohort size was well above the median number of patients in previous studies, attaining higher patient numbers would have allowed us to assess complication rates and outcomes better, especially within surgical technique subgroups and specifically within the staged orchidopexy group, which holds only 25 testicular units in 18 patients. Finally, our study reported on both inguinal orchidopexy and abdominal orchidopexy procedures combined, whereas most studies have reported on one treatment strategy only. We did, however, present outcomes for both procedures separately. It is our opinion that our report better reflects the common clinical practice of surgical centers where both surgical interventions are performed. documents.title: AUA Guideline on Nocturnal Enuresis Pediatric

chunks.content: Introduction Nocturnal enuresis (NE) is a prevalent condition among children characterized by involuntary urination during sleep [ , ]. Cross-national studies reveal significant regional variations in the prevalence of NE among children: European children aged 5–15 years show the highest prevalence at 12% [ – ], while India reports 11.89% among school-aged children (6–15 years) [ ]. The prevalence of NE in 5-year-old children in China is 15.13% and shows a decreasing trend with age [ , ]. Notably, Saudi Arabia exhibits the highest prevalence at 24% [ ]. The occurrence of NE is associated with various factors, including genetic, physiological, and psychological influences. Research has shown that children are at an increased risk of developing NE if their parents have a history of the condition [ ]. Furthermore, gender is a factor, with boys being more likely than girls to experience NE [ ]. In addition, it is reported that NE not only leads to varying degrees of psychosocial stress and diminished self-esteem in affected children but also contributes to anxiety among their parents or caregivers [ ]. Therefore, continued research into the early detection and intervention of NE is of vital importance for the future of our children populations. Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) in children and adolescents refers to a spectrum of breathing disorders occurring during sleep, ranging from primary snoring to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) [ ]. The most severe manifestation of SDB is obstructive OSA, characterized by recurrent partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep, resulting in abnormal ventilation and disrupted sleep patterns [ ]. The prevalence of sleep disorders in childhood is at least 25%-50%, with a peak incidence between the ages of 3 and 8 years [ , ]. The prevalence of pediatric OSA ranges from 1.2% to 5.7% [ ], and it is increasing alongside the rising trends of childhood obesity [ ]. These children typically exhibit adverse reactions, including attention deficits, behavioral and emotional issues, morning headaches, excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), and growth retardation [ ]. According to the International Classification of Sleep Disorders, Third Edition, the diagnosis of pediatric OSA is based on clinical history, an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) ≥ 1, and findings from polysomnography (PSG), which remains the gold standard for diagnosing OSA in children and adolescents [ , ]. Although there are many risk factors for NE, the relationship between NE and SDB remains ambiguous and debated in the existing literature. Both conditions are prevalent in pediatric populations and are associated with substantial long-term health consequences [ ]. Studies have shown that the prevalence of NE in children and adolescents aged 6–11 with OSA is 4.6%, with no significant difference between children without OSA [ ]. However, some studies have suggested mild SDB is not significantly correlated with NE, while severe OSA may significantly increase the risk [ ]. Different studies’ results are inconsistent, indicating the need for further research to elucidate this association. Although some studies have suggested an independent correlation between NE and severe SDB, such as OSA, there is still a lack of research focusing on the occurrence and relationship between NE and varying degrees of SDB. Therefore, this meta-analysis aimed to investigate the prevalence of SDB in participants with NE (SWN) and the prevalence of NE in participants with SDB (NWS) based on the available data and to determine the association between NE and different severities of SDB in 5–18 children. Methods Study selection and selection criteria This study followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 (PRISMA 2020) guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42024576610). A systematic search was conducted in four electronic databases: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane. The search included the keywords ‘Nocturnal Enuresis’ and ‘Sleep Apnea, Obstructive’ from database inception to 17 May 2024. Inclusion criteria required case-control, cohort, or cross-sectional studies involving populations with clearly defined diagnostic criteria for NE and/or OSA. Studies were excluded if they did not report or allow calculation of NE or OSA cases, lacked extractable data, or were literature reviews, case reports, animal studies, conference abstracts, or non-English publications. Data extraction Based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, two reviewers (YKL and SDS) independently assessed the eligibility of the studies, with final decisions made in consultation with an arbitrator (GWS). Data were extracted following standardized procedures, including details such as the first author, publication date, country, study design, sample source, sample size, mean age, gender ratio, methods used to assess NE and SDB (measurement techniques, diagnostic criteria, and thresholds), and all relevant covariates modifying the relationship between NE and SDB. The study’s primary outcomes were the pooled prevalence of NE and SDB, as well as the crude and adjusted effect estimates of the association between NE and SDB, expressed as ORs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Classification and

the studies, with final decisions made in consultation with an arbitrator (GWS). Data were extracted following standardized procedures, including details such as the first author, publication date, country, study design, sample source, sample size, mean age, gender ratio, methods used to assess NE and SDB (measurement techniques, diagnostic criteria, and thresholds), and all relevant covariates modifying the relationship between NE and SDB. The study’s primary outcomes were the pooled prevalence of NE and SDB, as well as the crude and adjusted effect estimates of the association between NE and SDB, expressed as ORs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Classification and diagnostic criteria for NE and SDB In this study, the study population comprises children and adolescents aged 5–18 years, and the term children and adolescents is used consistently throughout the manuscript to reflect this age range. Children and adolescents aged 5–18 years were included in this study. The diagnosis of NE in children and adolescents was primarily based on the International Children’s Continence Society (ICCS) criteria (used in 12 studies): urinary incontinence occurring ≥ 1 time/month for ≥ 3 months in children and adolescents aged ≥ 5 years, excluding organic causes. Other diagnostic criteria included: the Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ-22) in one study, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition, Text Revision (DSM IV-TR) in one study, the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) in one study, and the International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) in one study. Additionally, one study used a non-validated questionnaire. Two studies defined enuresis by frequency: one as ≥ 5 times per month (type unknown) and another as ≥ 3 times per week (type unknown). The cases of NE collected in this study were predominantly monosymptomatic enuresis (PMNE/MNE), and some studies did not distinguish subtypes. SDB was diagnosed primarily by PSG in 12 studies. Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) was diagnosed based on the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). In children and adolescents, OSAHS is typically defined as an AHI ≥ 1 event per hour, differing from adult criteria. The severity of OSAHS was categorized as mild (AHI 1–5 events/hour), moderate (AHI > 5–10 events/hour), and severe (AHI > 10 events/hour). However, specific AHI thresholds varied: two studies used the respiratory disturbance index (RDI) ≥ 1 event/hour. Additionally, three studies used the modified Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ-22), one study used the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-9-CM) criteria, and three studies diagnosed SDB based on frequent snoring (≥ 3 times per week) reported in questionnaires. One study used adenoid-nasopharyngeal ratio (ANR) ≥ 0.5, and another used both snoring questionnaire and ANR. Two studies employed the OSA-18 and PSQ-22 questionnaires. Research quality assessment The quality of each study was independently assessed by two researchers (YKL and SDS) using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for cohort and case-control studies, and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) scale for cross-sectional studies. The maximum score for cohort studies was 9, while for cross-sectional studies it was 11. Higher scores indicated better methodological quality, with studies scoring > 5 on NOS or > 8 on AHRQ considered of moderate to high reliability (Appendix S2). Any discrepancies were resolved through consultation with Guowei Si to reach a final decision. Statistical analyses This meta-analysis applied a random-effects model to obtain relatively conservative findings when significant heterogeneity was detected (I² > 50%, P < 0.05) based on the I² test. A fixed-effects model was used if no significant heterogeneity was observed (I² < 50%). Subgroup analyses were conducted to identify potential sources of heterogeneity. The quality and robustness of the results were assessed through sensitivity analyses. Additionally, publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s test. All data analyses were performed using Stata version 15.1 (StataCorp LLC, TX, USA, http://www.stata.com ). Results Literature retrieval and research traits The literature selection process is shown in Fig. , with 22 studies involving 40,296 patients included in the final analysis. The initially conducted database search identified 784 articles. After removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts based on inclusion and exclusion criteria, 469 articles were included. A full-text review of 53 articles resulted in the exclusion of 19 articles, leaving 34 articles for further assessment. Finally, 22 studies were included in the meta-analysis. Detailed search strategies are provided in Appendix S1. Articles were primarily excluded during the full-text review due to the inability to obtain complete data, even after contacting corresponding authors, or because the manuscript was not a formal research study (e.g., letters to the editor or conference abstracts). 10 studies focused on the prevalence of SWN, while 12 studies addressed the prevalence of NWS. No study reported both SWN and NWS prevalence simultaneously. Additionally, After excluding studies that failed to control for confounding factors or demonstrated methodological unreliability (e.g., high risk of bias in participant selection or outcome

Articles were primarily excluded during the full-text review due to the inability to obtain complete data, even after contacting corresponding authors, or because the manuscript was not a formal research study (e.g., letters to the editor or conference abstracts). 10 studies focused on the prevalence of SWN, while 12 studies addressed the prevalence of NWS. No study reported both SWN and NWS prevalence simultaneously. Additionally, After excluding studies that failed to control for confounding factors or demonstrated methodological unreliability (e.g., high risk of bias in participant selection or outcome measurement), 13 studies reporting adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were included in the final meta-analysis. Study characteristics Table summarizes the characteristics of the included studies. The studies were conducted across multiple countries and areas, including Italy (2 studies), Saudi Arabia (1), Indonesia (1), Australia (1), China (2), Egypt (3), Taiwan China (1), Brazil (1), Greece (3), Canada (1), Turkey (1), and the United States (5), spanning six continents: Europe, Asia, Oceania, Africa, North America, and South America. Most study populations were recruited from communities or outpatient clinics. 14 studies were cross-sectional, seven were case-control, and one was a cohort study. Among the included studies, the quality of 13 cross-sectional studies and six case-control studies was considered moderate to high, while the single cohort study was rated as high. Publication bias and sensitivity analysis Using Stata 15.1, funnel plots, Egger’s test and Begg’s test were performed to assess publication bias in the included studies. The results showed that both Egger’s test ( P = 0.601) and Begg’s test ( P = 0.322) for the OR values were non-significant ( P > 0.05), indicating no evidence of publication bias. For the prevalence of SWN, Egger’s test resulted in P = 0.000, but a supplementary Begg’s test yielded P = 0.170 ( P > 0.05), suggesting no significant publication bias. Similarly, Egger’s test showed P = 0.261 ( P > 0.05) for the prevalence of NWS, confirming the absence of significant publication bias. Sensitivity analysis further demonstrated the robustness of the results. Meta-analysis results Prevalence of SDB with NE results In a total sample of 5005 NE patients and 490 SDB patients, the pooled prevalence of SWN was 32.3% (95% CI: 0.283–0.362), with significant heterogeneity ( P < 0.001; I² = 98.1%; Fig. ). Table Presents the results of the subgroup analysis for the prevalence of SWN. The analysis showed that diagnostic criteria and assessment methods significantly influenced prevalence estimates. For studies diagnosing NE according to ICCS guidelines, the pooled prevalence was 48.7% (95% CI: 0.283–0.691), whereas those using ICD-9-CM reported only 1.6% (95% CI: 0.011–0.021). Similarly, differences were observed in SDB assessment methods. Studies using PSG and PSQ-22 yielded comparable prevalence estimates (51.2% and 52.8%, respectively), while studies applying ICD-9-CM criteria again showed much lower prevalence (1.6%). By study design, cross-sectional studies reported a higher pooled prevalence (41.6%) than case-control studies (13.6%). The study setting (community vs. hospital) did not substantially affect prevalence estimates. Sample size appeared to influence SWN prevalence: studies with small sample sizes (≤ 60) reported higher prevalence (61.3%), while very large studies (≥ 1000) showed markedly lower estimates (1.6%), suggesting a possible sample size effect. Regional differences were evident. The pooled prevalence was 2.0% in Asia, 32.9% in Europe, 52.8% in Africa, and 62.0% in America, indicating substantial variation across regions. Gender composition also appeared to affect prevalence. Studies with a female majority reported higher prevalence (49.0%) than those with a male majority (22.6%). One study with an unclear gender distribution showed a higher rate, but this result should be interpreted cautiously due to the single-study limitation. Overall, these findings suggest that methodological differences, regional factors, and gender composition contribute to the heterogeneity observed in the reported prevalence of SWN. Prevalence of NE with SDB results Among the included studies, a total of 6,254 SDB (OSA) cases and 1,434 NE cases were reported. The overall prevalence of NWS was 24.5% (95% CI: 0.157–0.333), with significant heterogeneity ( P < 0.001; I² = 98.8%; Fig. ). Table Summarizes the subgroup analysis results for NWS prevalence, showing how variations in diagnostic criteria, SDB assessment methods, study design, sample source, region, and gender contributed to the observed heterogeneity. Differences in NE diagnostic criteria were associated with notable variability in prevalence estimates. Studies applying the ICCS definition reported a pooled prevalence of 26.3% (95% CI: 0.142–0.366), whereas those using PSQ-22 yielded a lower estimate of 11.2% (95% CI: 0.098–0.126). Regarding SDB assessment, studies using PSG showed a pooled prevalence of 29.4% (95% CI: 0.161–0.426), while those employing snoring questionnaires (≥ 3 times/week) reported a markedly lower prevalence of 7.3% (95% CI: 0.053–0.093). Studies using ANR ≥ 0.5 criteria observed a higher prevalence of 30.7% (95% CI: 0.254–0.359), highlighting that methodological differences substantially influence

Studies applying the ICCS definition reported a pooled prevalence of 26.3% (95% CI: 0.142–0.366), whereas those using PSQ-22 yielded a lower estimate of 11.2% (95% CI: 0.098–0.126). Regarding SDB assessment, studies using PSG showed a pooled prevalence of 29.4% (95% CI: 0.161–0.426), while those employing snoring questionnaires (≥ 3 times/week) reported a markedly lower prevalence of 7.3% (95% CI: 0.053–0.093). Studies using ANR ≥ 0.5 criteria observed a higher prevalence of 30.7% (95% CI: 0.254–0.359), highlighting that methodological differences substantially influence NWS estimates. Study design had a limited effect on prevalence, with cross-sectional and case-control studies showing comparable results (25.0% vs. 23.3%). However, the study population contributed to significant differences: hospital-based studies reported higher prevalence (37.7% [95% CI: 0.191–0.564]) compared with community-based studies (13.6% [95% CI: 0.071–0.202]; P = 0.017). Marked regional differences were observed. The prevalence was lowest in South America (7.3%) and highest in Oceania (40.4%), followed by Europe (30.7%), North America (26.4%), and Asia (18.3%). Sample size did not appear to substantially affect results, with studies including ≥ 60 participants reporting 23.9% prevalence and those with < 60 reporting 28.2%. In terms of gender, studies with a female majority showed a slightly lower pooled prevalence (11.2% [95% CI: 0.055–0.169]) compared with male-majority studies (27.5% [95% CI: 0.153–0.396]), though differences were not statistically significant. Overall, these findings suggest that NWS prevalence varies considerably according to diagnostic definitions, SDB assessment tools, study populations, and regional factors, underscoring the methodological heterogeneity across studies. Odds ratio results We synthesized 16 adjusted effect sizes from 13 studies (32,367 participants, aged 5–18 years) were included to calculate the overall OR. The primary adjusted OR between SDB and NE was 2.85 (95% CI: 2.35–3.45; Fig. ). Sensitivity analysis excluding small-sample studies and those with unclear assessment criteria (e.g., Sakellaropoulou2012) substantially reduced heterogeneity (I² decreased from 73.4% to 43.8%) and confirmed result robustness (Fig. ). Table Subgroup analysis by diagnostic criteria revealed significant heterogeneity in the SDB-NE association ( P = 0.007). The strongest effects were observed with ICD-10 (OR = 5.81, 95% CI: 1.54–21.96) and PSQ-22 (OR = 4.81, 95% CI: 3.28–7.06). ICCS criteria showed a robust association (OR = 2.83, 95% CI: 2.52–3.17), while weaker effects were seen with ICD-9-CM (OR = 1.83, 95% CI: 1.25–2.68) and other criteria (OR = 2.23, 95% CI: 1.32–3.79). Similarly, subgroup analysis by SDB assessment method indicated significant heterogeneity ( P = 0.004). PSQ-22 again showed the strongest association (OR = 4.81, 95% CI: 3.28–7.06; single study), with robust associations for PSG (11 studies, OR = 2.78, 95% CI: 2.45–3.16, I² = 3.2%) and Questionnaire: snoring ≥ 3 times / week (2 studies, OR = 3.81, 95% CI: 2.07–7.02, I² = 0.0%), whereas ICD-9 criteria yielded weaker effects (OR = 1.83, 95% CI: 1.25–2.68, I² = 25.1%). Regardless of residential status, NE was identified as a risk factor for SDB, with ORs of 2.72 (95% CI: 2.04–3.64, I² = 65.7%) for community-based studies and 2.97 (95% CI: 2.25–3.91, I² = 12.7%) for hospitalized patients. Across study types, the results were consistent. Cross-sectional studies reported an adjusted OR of 2.98 (95% CI: 2.33–3.81), while case-control studies reported 2.82 (95% CI: 1.99–3.98). Similarly, studies focusing on SWN showed an OR of 3.02 (95% CI: 2.17–4.21, I² = 54.9%,), while those on NWS reported 2.75 (95% CI: 2.39–3.18, I² = 6.9%), with no significant difference between the two different exposure groups. Overall, SDB was associated with an increased risk of NE. The pooled ORs were 2.48 (95% CI: 1.68–3.67) for mild SDB, 2.91 (95% CI: 2.20–3.86) for moderate-to-severe SDB (I² = 26.6%), and 3.11 (95% CI: 1.70–5.68) for unclassified SDB (I² = 65.2%). No significant difference was observed across the severity subgroups ( P = 0.758). Regional differences in the association between SDB and NE were not statistically significant ( P = 0.747). The pooled ORs were 1.49 (95% CI: 0.95–2.35) for Asia-Pacific, 2.17 (95% CI: 1.38–3.42) for the Middle East, 2.34 (95% CI: 1.61–3.41) for America, and 2.98 (95% CI: 1.89–4.70) for Europe. For sample size, studies with > 60 participants reported an OR of 2.83 (95% CI: 2.30–3.50, I² = 53.1%), while those with ≤ 60 participants showed an OR of 3.20 (95% CI: 1.56–6.56, I² = 0.0%, P = 0.619). For gender, the pooled ORs were 2.49 (95% CI: 2.09–2.98) for male-majority studies, 4.38 (95% CI: 3.07–6.24) for female-majority studies, 1.89 (95% CI: 0.92–3.89) for gender-balanced studies, and 5.27 (95% CI: 3.15–8.83) for studies with unclear gender distribution ( P = 0.002). In the meta-analysis involving patients with SDB and NE, subgroup analyses were conducted to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. The results indicated that the strength of the association was significantly modified by the standardization level of

For gender, the pooled ORs were 2.49 (95% CI: 2.09–2.98) for male-majority studies, 4.38 (95% CI: 3.07–6.24) for female-majority studies, 1.89 (95% CI: 0.92–3.89) for gender-balanced studies, and 5.27 (95% CI: 3.15–8.83) for studies with unclear gender distribution ( P = 0.002). In the meta-analysis involving patients with SDB and NE, subgroup analyses were conducted to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. The results indicated that the strength of the association was significantly modified by the standardization level of diagnostic tools (particularly the NE and SDB assessment methods) and gender. Studies with female-majority populations or those using non-standardized diagnostic tools (e.g., ICD-10, PSQ-22, or unvalidated questionnaires) reported higher OR values. Study design, sample source, sample size, SDB severity, geographic region, and exposure group definition were not significant sources of between-subgroup heterogeneity. These variables had a significant impact on the estimates of both prevalence and ORs. Discussion This study represents the first systematic review and meta-analysis focusing on the prevalence of SWN and the prevalence of NWS, as well as the association between the two conditions. Based on 22 studies involving 40,296 participants, the pooled prevalence of SWN was 32.3%, while that of NWS was 24.5%. In addition, a significant association was observed between SDB and NE (pooled OR = 2.85), which remained robust after adjustment for potential confounders. Subgroup analyses further demonstrated that both mild SDB (primary snoring) and moderate-to-severe SDB (obstructive sleep apnea, OSA) were associated with an increased risk of NE, with comparable effect sizes. Although no clear dose-response relationship across SDB severity levels was identified, it is noteworthy that the point estimates numerically suggested a higher risk associated with moderate-to-severe SDB compared with mild SDB. This difference, however, did not reach statistical significance, which may reflect limited statistical power and heterogeneity across studies rather than a true absence of a biological gradient. Nevertheless, these findings indicate that even mild SDB may warrant clinical attention. Our results are consistent with previous studies reporting a higher prevalence of NE in children and adolescents with OSA. In a cross-sectional study, Brooks and Topol demonstrated that children with sleep apnea had a significantly higher prevalence of enuresis compared with controls [ ]. Similarly, Stone et al. reported that symptoms of sleep-disordered breathing were markedly more common among children with nocturnal enuresis, supporting the role of SDB as a potential contributing factor to NE [ ]. For example, Andreu-Codina et al. [ ] found that NE was significantly more common in pediatric patients with OSA than in healthy controls, and that children with coexisting OSA and NE exhibited more pronounced craniofacial abnormalities. Previous studies have suggested that potential mechanisms linking sleep-disordered breathing to nocturnal enuresis may involve recurrent nocturnal arousals, intermittent hypoxemia, and autonomic nervous system dysregulation, all of which may affect lower urinary tract function and bladder control [ – ]. Although the pooled prevalence of SWN appeared numerically higher than that of NWS, this difference did not reach statistical significance, suggesting that the observed discrepancy may largely reflect heterogeneity in study populations and diagnostic criteria rather than a true biological difference. Previous studies have shown that children with NE tend to experience deeper sleep and greater difficulty with arousal, which may predispose them to SDB [ , ]. These findings suggest that the appa rent bidirectional relationship between SDB and NE is more plausibly explained by common underlying pathways, particularly impaired arousal mechanisms, autonomic nervous system dysregulation, and sleep fragmentation rather than two independent causal directions [ ]. Moreover, variations in diagnostic standards substantially influenced prevalence estimates. For instance, SWN prevalence ranged widely depending on whether NE was defined using ICCS criteria or administrative codes, and SDB prevalence differed markedly between studies using polysomnography and those relying on diagnostic coding systems. These findings highlight the importance of standardized definitions when interpreting prevalence data. Geographic subgroup analyses revealed no significant regional differences in the strength of the association between SDB and NE, indicating that this relationship is relatively consistent across populations. Interestingly, gender-stratified analyses suggested a stronger association in studies predominantly involving girls compared with those focusing mainly on boys. Although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear, hormonal influences during childhood and early adolescence may partly contribute to sex-related differences in sleep regulation and bladder control [ ]. In addition to hormonal factors, sex-specific differences in neuroendocrine regulation, including central arousal pathways and autonomic nervous system control, may also play an important role in modulating the interaction between sleep-disordered breathing and bladder function. However, these mechanisms remain insufficiently explored and warrant further investigation. Evidence from diverse countries further supports the global relevance of SDB–NE comorbidity.
